In this study, we investigate the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks in solving high-dimensional eigenvalue problems in the Schrödinger equation. We establish theoretical bounds on the spectral bias of these networks, which demonstrate their tendency to prioritize lower eigenvalues over higher ones. We also investigate the influence of network capacity on this spectral bias, revealing that increased capacity tends to result in convergence towards the ground state eigenvalue. Our findings are supported by experimental results showing the spectral bias in training processes and its correlation with generalization error.

The highest energy cosmic rays exhibit significant variations, and understanding these fluctuations is crucial for exploring the origins of ultra-high energy cosmic rays, which exhibit significant anisotropy. Observatories like the Pierre Auger Observatory, located in the Northern Hemisphere, have detected large-scale variations and are expected to detect even more significant patterns as their sensitivity improves. Research involving data collected by Pierre Auger between 2004 and 2013, covering the energy range of 10 to 55 EeV, has shown substantial fluctuations at 28 EeV, with a significance level of 5.8 sigma. This study utilized two methods to analyze fluctuations, including the angular power spectrum analysis and the log ratio method, both of which yielded consistent results. The observations suggest energy-dependent variations, and future analyses with expanded datasets are anticipated to clarify this phenomenon, offering insights into the cosmic ray sources above 10 EeV.

This note aims to clarify and expand upon the results presented in the authors' previous work, specifically concerning the homogeneous limit of thin films with layered periodic microstructures and incommensurable periods that converge from above to one another.

This research explores the possibilities of self-interacting Dirac particles within the framework of Flat FLRW spacetime. The conducted analysis reveals that within this framework, only one type of self-interaction is feasible, thus significantly limiting the scope of theoretical and physical applications. As a consequence, the corresponding quantum equations no longer admit a time-independent solution and instead yield complex energy expressions. Furthermore, the resulting wave function indicates that the FLRW background induces a quenching of quark flavor symmetry.

Training deep learning models on histopathology images, specifically for identifying tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, is hindered by challenges related to data accessibility, annotation complexity, and expert scarcity. A novel approach utilizes federated learning to train deep neural networks for a category expansion task, which involves training on histology images to recognize a base set of histological elements, and then being deployed to identify novel elements on individual institutions' datasets without accessing the underlying data. By training on over 50,000 hematoxylin and eosin stained images, this method was successful in training a robust federated model that accurately detected novel cell types on test datasets of over 10,000 images. The outcome demonstrates the potential of federated learning in training reliable models for complex medical image analysis tasks.

Recent advancements in two-dimensional magnetic substances have made it possible to explore novel quantum phenomena involving spin-wave magnons and phonons, both of which play a crucial role in defining these materials' unique properties. These characteristics can be exploited through the framework of cavity magnomeathics to generate magnon-phonon hybrid states. By incorporating the cavity magnonics drive, it becomes feasible to create two-dimensional magnetic substance quantum states by two means: either through two-photon processes mediated by both a magnon and a phonon, or via the Kerr nonlinearity produced by the spin-Hall effect. These methods give rise to distinct characteristics; the former method generates oscillatory magnon-phonon hybrid states, while the latter results in Kerr cat states. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that two-dimensional magnetic substances may facilitate the creation of coherent magnon-phonon-photonic states through three-photon interactions, highlighting their potential in developing quantum technologies.

Using reinforcement learning to develop physical agents poses a major challenge in robotics and biology.  Most reinforcement learning frameworks face a fundamental issue: they lack a starting point for evolution, hindering their ability to evolve complex behaviors.  The proposed framework REGE addresses this limitation by integrating an evolutionary algorithm to automatically generate pathways for reinforcement learning to follow.  These pathways enable the environment to provide more effective rewards and prevent agents from getting stuck in local optima.  The framework's capabilities have been demonstrated through evolution and movement learning of a quadrupedal robot resembling a dog.

The 30-meter telescope's High-Resolution Spectrograph Mode observed a low-luminosity active galactic nucleus in NGC 7213.  For a 100,000 seconds exposure,  observations were conducted  in two modes:  one covering 0.50-2.00 keV and the other 0.30-10.00 keV.  The 0.50-2.00 keV data revealed significant absorption by intervening gas at a massive amount,  $log_{10}(X_H) = 21.42^{+1.08}_{-0.85}$ cm$^{-2}$,  which was  in 2 other low-luminosity active galactic nuclei with similar absorption values.  However,  the  observed  broad absorption features were  not supported by the 0.30-10.00 keV data.  Instead,  this mode revealed no significant absorption and  revealed  two broad emission features at 0.46 and 0.53 keV with a  possible cool gas temperature,  $log_{10}(T_s) = 6.14^{+0.30}_{-0.24}$,  and  a  surface  brightness of  $2 \times 10^{-13}$ erg cm$^{-2}$

Model-based optimal control regulators are well-established and effective, 
but depend on an accurate system model, which can be difficult and expensive 
to obtain. Model-free alternatives, such as reinforcement learning, are 
successful in configuring nonlinear regulators without a system model, 
but are computationally intensive and may struggle with hyperparameter 
selection. Our proposal presents an efficient solution that combines the 
advantages of model-free learning with configuration simplicity, even for 
complex systems. Our approach comprises two distinct phases: the first 
involves learning a parameterized control policy, and the second utilizes the 
obtained parameters to optimize the control gains, similar to a model-based 
regulator, but with enhanced performance due to the inclusion of learned system characteristics. Our method guarantees convergence to optimal performance, 
and we demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical examples in optimal configuration, with results showing significant computational savings and improved performance.

For the future SiD SiD detector concept, initial silicon sensor production techniques involve the use of n+-type material. However, recent research explored the feasibility of p+-type alternative using the energy separation method. This paper examines the silicon sensor performance difference resulting from various bulk and contact types. The outcomes suggest that PEMC and TEM methods yield the best potential for both n and p types, with p+ types exhibiting improved potential due to better resistivity separation and unchanged voltage requirements.

The CAOS project's third paper introduces Tomographic Plot (TOP), a new approach to 3D mapping of stellar populations using spectroscopic data from different wavelengths and surveys. Using TOP, we re-examine Tonantzintla 2 (Ton2), a nearby globular cluster with known chemical variations, and determine its three-dimensional metallicity and alpha-element abundance across the cluster with high precision. Ton2's core is found to have a narrow range of metallicty and alpha-element abundance, while these quantities vary linearly toward the cluster's outer regions. The cluster core lies within the plane defined by [Fe/H] = -0.50 ± 0.03 and [α/Fe] = +0.20 ± 0.03, while its outer regions are found to have a relationship between [Fe/H] and [α/Fe] with a slope of -0.30 ± 0.03. The cluster's structure is then compared to other Tonantzintla cluster data, and its core's location in the CAOS plane is explored. The results of our study provide a new perspective on the dynamics and chemical evolution of Ton2.

Earth-observing datasets have grown to massive scales, hindering the progress of 
research in data-rich deep learning due to data collection and preparation 
bottlenecks. While distributed data storage and efficiency enhancements help 
temporarily mitigate these issues, they do not fully resolve the problem. To 
address this issue, a new approach is needed to manage and process the data 
more effectively, taking full advantage of modern computational capabilities. 
To this end, we introduce EarthNets, a network of data centers specializing in 
planet observation that enables R&D by providing benchmarking, optimization, 
and efficiency solutions. By coordinating access to computing resources and 
datasets, EarthNets accelerates and simplifies research, allowing multiple 
projects to leverage the same infrastructure while promoting innovation and 
advancement in planet observation-related research and development.

To better understand the behavior of active nematic fluids, which are characterized by their distinct phase transitions and life-like properties, we employ the method of dynamic renormalization group analysis. Starting primarily from the Kennedy-Toner-Tu reformulation of the active nematics equations, which are three-dimensional, we examine the behavior of the most significant fluctuation parameters via detailed fixed point and exponent flow calculations within the renormalization group method. Our findings, which are supported by previous renormalization group studies, reveal that these fluctuation parameters are capable of being captured by the active nematics equations, resulting in qualitatively accurate predictions of the observations reported in active nematics experiments. We also explore the effects of alternative reformulations, which are two-dimensional versions of the active nematics equations, on the renormalization group analysis. These reformulations, which are motivated by the hydrodynamics formulation of active nematics, lead to additional relevant variables when subjected to renormalization group analysis. Despite this variability, our findings, which are characterized by simple linear beta functions, suggest that these additional variables do not significantly affect the ultimate outcome of the renormalization group flow.

In real-world applications of regression algorithms, output quality can be severely compromised when data contains anomalies. Most anomaly detection methods are tailored to supervised learning contexts, where historical data is available for reference. However, in unsupervised scenarios with limited or no historical data, new data points with distinct characteristics may emerge, posing a significant challenge. This paper introduces a framework called ReAD, which detects local anomalies in regression tasks by dividing the dataset into manageable partitions and analyzing each one separately. By leveraging the characteristics of each partition, including its size and shape, regression models can be fine-tuned to reflect the underlying data trends. This research also compares various partitioning strategies and demonstrates the effectiveness of ReAD using multiple datasets from actual research and industry applications.

In a previous study, its methodology is building upon which the current research calculates the pion vector shape factor, $F_\pi(Q^2)$, using lattice QCD simulations at three distinct lattice spacings and three unmixed quark masses. By combining simulations at three different strange quark masses with three different lattice spacings, we are able to verify the reliability of our results in the deep Euclidean region through the Bernsteins' theorem. Our analysis shows that our results are in good agreement with both experimental data and other theoretical models. Specifically, our study finds that radiative corrections to the pion vector form factor contribute approximately $-0.64$ ppm to the $(g-2)$ measurement, representing about 40 percent of its previous estimation.

Representation learning for code serves as a fundamental prerequisite for developing code-based AI applications, yet it remains relatively underexplored compared to natural language. While prior research has focused on image or text, code necessitates a more comprehensive view that captures both semantic functionality and underlying structural relationships. To address this challenge, we introduce FNGR, an innovative transformer model that regresses a set of global features, reflecting key code characteristics, in contrast to existing approaches that rely on predicting a single vector. Evaluated on three diverse datasets - Python LAMBO, Java LAMBO, and EC2, our model is successfully applied to tasks including defect detection and code similarit, yielding improved accuracy and surpassing state-of-the-art models.

Our research examines how a galaxy's morphology influences the relationship between its stellar mass and the mass of its surrounding halo. Using high-resolution simulations from the Moving Mesh Galaxy Formation project, which feature detailed gas and stellar distributions, we determined this connection by fitting exponential light profiles to a subset of our simulated galaxies based on their morphology type. The analysis reveals that disc galaxies have distinct characteristics compared to spheroidal galaxies, particularly in how their stellar mass relates to their surrounding halo mass. Specifically, in disc galaxies, this relationship peaks at intermediate mass ratios, whereas the relationship in spheroidal galaxies does not show such a trend. Moreover, we found that this relationship tends to peak at higher mass ratios as these galaxies evolve into more massive systems, and we observe a trend in which relationships beyond peak mass ratio tend to plateau at the scale of a few times 10^11 solar masses.

Optical limiting magnitude achieved at astronomical observatories is heavily influenced by the total optical depth caused by aerosols and clouds in the atmosphere. These factors also dictate the calibration of astronomical photometric systems, which in turn are utilized to calculate the total columnar aerosol optical depth through photometric calibration refinement. This technique is now being utilized to monitor air quality in non-astronomical applications as well. Clouds significantly reduce optical depth measurements; however, utilizing data from variable stars with high brightness can help filter out cloud interference. Our team has been using satellite data alongside astronomical observations to determine optimal locations for OHP-CAT telescope installation in aerosol monitoring, which involved integrating meteorological information and satellite imagery to assess data quality and assess the utility of these measurements in identifying low-altitude air masses. Our analysis also included evaluating the suitability of using photometric calibration of multiple variable stars or a combination of stellar magnitude data and satellite observations to estimate aerosol optical depth.

The GGLasso package is a Python implementation of the Generalized Graphical Lasso, which can analyze datasets with non-Gaussian data and outliers using the Maximum Likelihood Estimation and a Cayley smoothing technique on the covariance matrix. This package includes two methods for estimating a precision matrix, one based on Python's CVXPY optimizer and another based on Banerjee's algorithm with an O(p^3) complexity. A notable advantage of the GGLasso package is its support for complex data types, such as complex numbers and Manifold data. The package also provides functions for computing manifold-based covariance and precision matrices, such as the Oviedo-Espino method. Finally, the GGLasso package supports various alternative loss functions and regularization methods to improve performance on diverse datasets.

The two dominant theories explaining gas loss from protoplanetary disks, planetesimal disk formation, are planetesimal-driven MHD disk breeze and stellar mass loss. We anticipate that future high-resolution radio observations from the ALMA telescope will enable us to distinguish between these models by comparing the radial distribution of ions at 1 mm with those at longer wavelengths. We demonstrate that, for the TW Hydrae system, radio observations at 1 mm will distinguish between these models, but require significantly higher spatial resolution than those currently available from ALMA. Specifically, if TW Hydrae follows the predictions of a planetesimal-driven disk breeze model, its ion radial distribution should significantly differ from that seen in ALMA dust continuum scans. Nonetheless, if gas loss is primarily due to stellar mass loss, the ion distribution may not significantly differ from what ALMA observes.

This research introduces an entirely unsupervised method for identifying the tone and voiced-unvoiced status of speech signals. The approach utilizes the autoregressive speech signal model, whose parameters are estimated via the Yule-Walker method. For tone tracking, we utilize the ReckonTone system, incorporating a simplified Kalman filter for efficient real-time tone detection. Similarly, we developed a basic Kalman filter for voiced-unvoised status detection, which successfully identifies UV switches. Notably, our experiments demonstrated that the proposed system's performance on the ToNeINuS database matches that of the ReckonTone system, and future enhancements could leverage dynamic kernel bandwidth adjustment to improve tonal tracking accuracy.

We introduce a new forward-backward algorithm to tackle monotone inclusions with a mix of Lipschitz continuous operators and monotone operators, which cannot be effectively addressed by existing algorithms in this category. Drawing inspiration from the Jourda's inertial forward-backward method and the Krasnoselskii-Mann theorem, we integrate dynamical weighting to ensure convergence. This method capitalizes on the gap between the Lipschitz constant of the continuous operator and the monotonicity constant of the remaining operator to propose an efficient dynamical parametric inertial scheme. Furthermore, we extend this approach to solve convex minimization problems by deriving a corresponding dynamical primal-dual algorithm.

This research explores loop corrections to Higgs particle masses within a non-supersymmetric model, combining the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric model (NMSSM) with a Type-I reverse seesaw mechanism for neutrino mass generation. The models studied vary in additional neutrino doublet placement, within or outside the Higgs sector. A crucial feature is the absence of large neutrino masses coupling to loops involving third-generation fermi particles. As such, these models exhibit naturally occurring loop corrections aligning with experimental findings. The focus is on models with minimal particle content, specifically analyzing one- and two-loop effects on Higgs masses and assessing their stability. The study identifies regions of parameter space consistent with neutrino oscillation data and is particularly interested in a specific model containing two extra singlet neutrinos. This involves detailed calculations of loop corrections and is done using the framework of Feynman diagrams generated by the tool 'FeynArtms'.

Achieving optimal results in neural network architecture design requires careful consideration of numerous factors, such as training duration and model accuracy, which often involve navigating a vast property space. In contrast to conventional geneticalgorithm-based approaches that ignore many of these properties or address them in a sequential manner, our methodology employs Property Directed Synthesis to systematically explore all relevant design spaces by incorporating genetic algorithms within its framework. As a result, our approach is capable of discovering novel architectures with superior performance, even when optimizing complex models like ResNet, which ultimately yields better results than methods like Evolutionary Architecture Search.

In the future of wireless communication, millimeter wave (mmWave) systems will rely on multi-group broadcasting to enhance energy efficiency and network capacity. This approach involves transmitting a single data stream that can be received by multiple groups, each utilizing hyper-dimensional processing to decode its respective group's information. However, simultaneous broadcasting often requires hybrid encoding schemes. This study investigates various mmWave broadcasting methods, comparing their suitability across different scenarios, and explores the impact of hybrid encoding strategies on multi-group broadcasting performance.

Federated Learning creates a collaborative and privacy-preserving collaborative model by training multiple clients simultaneously. However, the process is slowed down by communication inefficiencies between the server and clients. A novel communication-efficient communication protocol called Federated Knowledge Distillation introduces interactivity between the server and clients. Firstly, the server sends random knowledge to clients, which then train on local data and send updated representations to the server. Next, the server aggregates these representations and distributes them back to the clients, allowing them to perform additional training, after which the process repeats. Notably, this approach achieves comparable model accuracy to efficient methods like FedAvg with minimal data exchanges. Furthermore, we introduce a novel analysis showing that knowledge representation and the server play a crucial role in Federated Learning, informing future design decisions.

Decentralized decision-making in large-scale networks of autonomous nodes can result in excessive latency due to multi-hop routing, especially in systems integrating Near Data Storage and Edge Computing capabilities. We utilize Named Data Networking (NDN) as a framework for coordination and propose the concept of Ideal Dynamic Coordination (IDC), which involves the optimal sequencing of tasks and storage units along a path to minimize delays in a network where tasks can be split and stored units are operated by autonomous entities seeking to maximize profit. We develop a stochastic model to identify conditions under which IDC remains stable and efficient, and we simulate various strategies for operation and profit optimization by autonomous storage managers, showing that competing IDCs can coexist in equilibrium even when their priorities differ.

Recent research by the authors demonstrated the stability of an elongated Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped network with two balanced arms. Now, we consider a modified beam where the outer nodes are positioned at exponentially increased distances from the central node. Using a transformation that adapts to this configuration, we develop a new coordinate system and prove its unitary nature. Next, we analyze the spectrum of the associated generator, revealing it contains only imaginary eigenvalues, which can be estimated at order $n$. Through these findings, we conclude that the dynamics on the star-formed graph are unitary and hyperbolic, effectively addressing scenarios where the outer nodes' distances dominate even at high frequencies.

In the quark-meson model incorporating explicit chiral asymmetry breaking, we analyze how asymmetry influences quark matter and how it affects the behavior of quark matter from the perspective of color superconductivity. The breaking of chiral asymmetry leads to a significant reduction in the critical charge density threshold beyond which nonuniform phases emerge, and our findings indicate that a third-order phase transition can occur in the quark-meson model with explicit chiral asymmetry breaking.

Recent theoretical studies have predicted a new type of topological insulators composed of three layers: one single atomic layer on both sides and a wider gap one in the middle. To identify these topological insulators, researchers utilized first-principles calculations to analyze the electronic properties and stability of MTl4Te3 compounds in the cubic and hexagonal crystal structures. The analysis showed that the materials are dynamically and energetically stable and that they possess unique properties: a 0.72 eV band gap in the hexagonal structure and entirely p-character electronic frameworks in both structures. The notable surface states exhibited by the materials exhibit quadratic dispersion and distinct Dirac cones on both surfaces.

Optimizing complex systems often involves adjusting parameters within an unknown objective function. When multiple performance criteria are considered simultaneously, the optimization process becomes even more difficult due to the absence of information about the objective function's structure. Despite the absence of such information, the optimization process can be facilitated by effectively combining prior information about data trends and the location of the Pareto-optimal front using utility function-based methods. To improve this process, our research enhances utility function learning through the development of new techniques: smooth utility functions for smoother Pareto-optimal front approximation, disutility functions for easier evaluation of inferior solutions and their rejection, and utility function transferability for sharing information across parametric optimizations with different objectives. These new capabilities are demonstrated in the optimization of multi-objective benchmark problems and real-world systems, including the design of mechanical systems and the investigation of gene expression in cancer research.

In the realm of adversarial machine learning, generating blackbox attacks on reinforcement learning models poses a significant challenge. Traditional methods like decision-based attacks require numerous interactions with the environment, which could significantly impact real-world applications. To overcome this limitation, our approach uses an adversary agent to approximate the temporal information of actions taken by the target policy. By leveraging this estimated temporal information, our attack strategy enhances the adversarial action sequence generation by exploiting the model's reliance on past action timings. By incorporating a gradient-free decision-based attack, we successfully devised two attack techniques: one without and another without considering the estimated temporal information. Experimental results demonstrate that our attack method without using the estimated temporal information yields slightly better success rates but requires more queries. Conversely, our approach using the estimated temporal information appears most effective when considering recent past action timings (up to three actions). Overall, our findings demonstrate that considering estimated temporal information leads to significant improvements in blackbox attack success rates on reinforcement learning models.

Our investigation focuses on the electronic properties of 2D crystalline models exhibiting non-symmorphic symmetry. By examining various systematic adjustments within the electronic band structure, such as altering electronic doping and applying external strain, we explore their profound impact on Dirac points within the framework of non-symmorphic symmetry. These examinations uncover that Dirac points can only be stabilized in certain wallpaper groups and that both demagnetization and strain can effectively remove them. Furthermore, we identify a systematic method for fine-tuning the locations of Dirac points across the Brillouin zone through both magnetic doping and external strain applications. Notably, our results also demonstrate the potential for inducing stable linear dispersion in Dirac points from graphitic electronic behavior via strain applications, thereby providing a pathway to creating materials with exceptional transport properties while preserving their magnetic characteristics.

In the realm of Risk-aware Reinforcement Learning (RL), exploring non-stationary sub-Riemannian environments, such as traffic flow and geodesic navigation, poses significant challenges. To overcome this, we introduce a novel model, $\beta$-ORL, capable of adapting to dynamic changes while also measuring and controlling fluctuation risks. Our model enables the dynamic regret to grow at a nearly optimal rate and allows for control parameters to simultaneously control risk and regret. Additionally, we propose a new risk indicator function and develop a novel identification method to identify the changes in the landscape and design the exploration process. Our approach decouples identification and optimal policy learning through a separation design. Our theoretical analysis confirms that the identification method achieves optimal performance and has a low threshold for detecting changes. Our simulation results validate the effectiveness of our model and approach.

The widespread adoption of collaborative work platforms has led to the world of work 2.0 by enabling teams to manage their projects online using various datasets stored in project tracking systems like Jira. These datasets contain information about project management data, allowing researchers to study topics such as requirement analysis, bug reporting, and software development processes. However, these datasets are only accessible for a limited time, hindering replication studies and future research advancements. To address this issue, we utilized publicly available Jira data through the JiraWatch API to create an extensive dataset containing problem tracking information, which includes issues created during the COVID-19 pandemic across 200 projects resulting in over 300,000 entries. Our research provides insights into the characteristics of these data and compares their key metrics with previously used project tracking data, in addition to analyzing issues related to software development processes.

In distributed machine learning, large datasets are often partitioned across multiple nodes for training purposes. However, partitioning training data significantly hinders model performance due to the reliance on linear aggregation functions that fail to capture complex patterns effectively. To address this limitation, we propose AggFuncOpt, a novel optimization approach that optimizes a non-linear aggregation function while maintaining partition independence. Our method demonstrates that partition independence is achievable under specific conditions, and experimental results on various datasets validate its efficacy in achieving better model performance and convergence rates in both convex and non-convex training scenarios.

We developed and simulated an integrated system using only one small yttrium atom placed near a laser-driven cavity to capture, manipulate, and measure the atom through a process known as sideband cooling. Our approach employs a C-shaped arrangement of three sets of diffraction traps created by a specialized interference pattern, forming a grid-like structure that confines the atom within a specific plane. We demonstrated that this arrangement effectively captures the atom and stabilizes it in a particular quantum state, where we then use a series of controlled laser pulses to move the atom and apply logical operations to it. To read out the atom's quantum state, we first move it into the C-shaped cavity and measure its emitted light. Our proposed method has a high fidelity of 99.99% for executing quantum gates and 99.9% for measuring the atom's quantum state, outperforming traditional methods in both cases. Our novel approach offers the advantage of performing all operations on a single atom without the need for precise positioning systems.

Let the free monoid over an ordered alphabet be denoted as $\Lambda^*$ and the set of its strictly increasing sequences as $I(\Lambda^*)$. The set of increasing completion of $\Lambda^*$ is represented as $\Lambda^{\ast}\langle I(\Lambda^*)\rangle$. To establish the equivalence between the set of increasing completion and an equivalent definition based on infinite strictly increasing sequences in $\Lambda^{\ast}\langle I(\Lambda^*)\rangle$, denoted as $S(\Lambda^*)$, we first demonstrate that $S(\Lambda^*)$ satisfies the conditions to complete $\Lambda^*$. Furthermore, we derive a characterization of $S(\Lambda^*)$ using only strictly increasing sequences in $\Lambda^*$.

Traditional polymer models rely on simplistic assumptions of random selection, linear averaging and exclusive adaptation. Due to their ease of use, these models have been widely employed, yet their underlying premises are not supported by reality as evidenced by numerous studies. To better understand the relationship between composition and properties, this study presents a novel technique to derive polymer formulas from compositional data using linear regression and integer optimization. The proposed technique facilitates the identification of all feasible formulas matching specified constraints, with the goal of determining which polymers are most likely to be synthesized in reality. The study utilizes a comprehensive dataset of over 13000000000 potential formulas to validate its findings. Results indicate that existing models fail to accurately predict compositional trends across multiple properties and that the polymers they propose are rarely produced during actual synthesis. To address this discrepancy, the study suggests a new synthesis probability assessment based on the degree of compositional freedom. Notably, the study finds that the polymers generated through actual synthesis fall within a smaller range of compositions compared to the total feasible polymers. The study's findings highlight a need for the polymer community to collect synthetic data and the desired composition must be precisely defined before conducting any studies involving polymers with a target property.

In the field of Model-Based Systems Engineering, creating highly reliable software and hardware systems involves modeling complex systems and making data-driven decisions. One critical area within this field is breathing synchronization during anesthesia, which significantly impacts surgical procedures. Researchers have been trying to find an optimal level of sedation that allows patients to breathe naturally without the need for synchronized breathing patterns. However, there have been challenges in making these strategies effective due to the inability to control breathing patterns completely. This research suggests using direct transcription for dynamic breathing control by creating an accurate breathing model and adjusting sedation levels in real-time to improve breathing efficiency. Although this approach has been proposed, there have been a lack of clear guidelines on how to implement it within a Model-Based Systems Engineering framework. This research addresses this gap by providing a step-by-step guide on how to develop and refine an breathing model, which leads to an optimal control strategy for real-time sedation adjustment. This sedation adjustment is integrated into an anesthesiometer prototype, which has been tested in an Anesthesia Control Competition, leading to improved breathing regularity and more efficient breathing patterns in two different patients. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of direct transcription within a Model-Based Systems Engineering framework, and highlights its potential to contribute to an optimal breathing adjustment policy, which may help address the ongoing challenges related to breathing synchronization during anesthesia.

Building upon Baker and Tiwari's concept of platform groups for bicritical rational functions on $\mathbb{P}^1$, we explore the universal property of these group sequences and establish that they originate from an optimal function iteration sequence. Furthermore, we demonstrate the uniqueness of this group sequence and infer that any rational function with platform groups matching those of a function $f$ is a composition of $f$ with a compatible endomorphism of $\mathbb{P}^1$.

In the context of a high-dimensional linear regression model, our objective is to analyze a simplistic Bayesian approach where the prior distribution for regression coefficients depends on empirical data derived from a separate training set. An asymptotic framework involving sequential learning processes has been developed where the training set size grows independently of the sample size, our main finding showing that a posterior concentration phenomenon occurs under broad assumptions, especially when using pre-established priors. As a result, Bayesian methods demonstrate model selection consistency where coefficients determined to be non-zero remain stable over time and accurately capture the true model. Additionally, our findings indicate that this approach yields valid statistical inferences even in the absence of knowledge about the variability of errors, specifically by establishing asymptotic normality for Bayesian confidence intervals which maintain first-order accuracy.

High-performance machining centers are costly investments for manufacturing companies, thus it's essential to choose the most energy-efficient options. By integrating power management into the machine selection process, enterprises can optimize energy usage, lower operational costs, and minimize their environmental impact. To address this, a novel approach based on Bayesian evaluation and genetic enhancement is developed to predict the power consumption of various machining centers, enabling a precise evaluation of their energy efficiency. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated using a dataset of 10 machining centers, resulting in a high accuracy of 93% in comparing theoretical and actual power usage.

The existence and uniqueness of an Ahlfors regular conformal measure with a specific exponent on a locally finite connected infinite graph are investigated, with the exponent being determined by the spectral dimension of the random walk on the same graph. Our analysis demonstrates that such a measure must exist under certain conditions, and its conformal factor is necessarily 1 in those instances. However, we also find instances where a regular measure may fail to exist despite a prior conformal measure being present, highlighting the complexity of this phenomenon. Moreover, we establish that the measure is unique when it does exist and is equal to the counting measure under certain conditions, arising from zero spectral dimension where branching occurs at every point, while on trees or other non-branching graphs the measure is equal to the capacity of the Green function.

Using the approach that blends η-η' in the vector meson channel, we calculate fφ, 
fS, and mS corresponding to the physical state of the φ meson. We determine 
the parameter k by considering both the Gaudin rule and the requirement that 
does not introduce strange quarks into the φ meson. Both methods yield the 
same result of k ≈ 3. With this value, our findings align with experimental data 
for the masses of the η and η' mesons as well as their decay constants. We calculate 
the decay constants of the φ meson and obtain mS, the mixing angle for the S state,
 demonstrating that our results agree with available experimental data. We calculate 
the content of q̃, S, and N in the φ meson and find that the S content is approximately 
30% with no N content. We verify our results using the Gaudin rule and the 
principle that excludes strange quarks from the φ meson.

This study investigates both unique and complex online signature templates using established statistics on time-series data. A substantial library of 3,960 Italian online signatures was gathered through a collaborative effort. For each individual, three distinct signatures were created on an electronic device equipped with a resistive touch screen. We leverage statistical measures to assess the templates' intricacy and repeatability through computed indices. The analysis compares the frequencies of the gathered indices to assess their distribution across the population. Furthermore, we utilize non-parametric statistical tests to examine the relationship between index values and indices' intricacy levels, respectively.

We investigate the string theory vacuum in six dimensions, leveraging the properties of the orbifold from the perspective of superconformal algebra to analyze the non-asymmetric sector's contribution to the elevated-derivative tree-level vacuum amplitude. By examining the mechanism behind the asymptotic behavior of this amplitude, particularly whether it exhibits soft factorization, insights are gained for understanding the nature of vacuum amplitudes in less than four dimensions, especially in models featuring asymmetric orbifolds. Furthermore, this study provides foundational knowledge for developing non-renormalization theorems within the context of asymmetric orbifold models.

Our research reveals that introducing a charge defect into a two-dimensional cholesteric liquid crystal with chiral molecules leads to higher-order patterns of spin-vortex associations, accompanied by an increased number of spin deflections and associated momentum changes. These higher-order associations are associated with systems featuring complex topology and utilize both first and second topological charges, which are linked to orbital and spin deflections respectively. Through our findings, we uncover an association between this type of liquid crystal systems' optical properties and their hidden momentum, which may offer potential applications in the field of photonic devices.

One of the main elements in the universe, hydrogen, is found in various forms such as molecular, atomic, and other compounds in the ISM. The balance between these forms is affected by the environment, including the environment of the local interstellar cloud where the solar system originated. To understand this process, researchers look at various isotopes of elements like deuterium and other unusual forms of hydrogen. Multilingual individuals face a variety of language options when communicating online, which significantly impacts their choices. Despite their numerous platforms for expression, their text messages have not been fully explored by researchers. Texts that combine multiple languages are known as code-mixed, resulting from the coexistence of two or more languages. They develop from language blending and are prevalent in internet communication, often appearing without a clear boundary between language types. Research on code-switching has shifted towards exploring its NLP applications in communities that use multiple languages, focusing on specific language pairs like English and other languages. However, this direction may not effectively address the needs of multilingual community members who engage in text mixing rather than simple code-switching. We will explore more effective research paths for supporting internet text messages that mix English and non-English languages, focusing on challenges, constraints, motivations, and the potential of NLP in multiple languages.

Biomedical graph modeling has emerged as a prominent approach for tackling complex challenges in bioinformatics and medicine. By accurately depicting diverse networks and their relationships, theoretical models enable the formulation of novel scientific hypotheses. Yet, determining which model best fits the data often proves to be an arduous, time-consuming process. This review outlines recent breakthroughs in using graph neural networks for representing biomedical graphs, both theoretical and empirical. It highlights the utility of GNNs in bridging the gap between the latent properties of biomedical entities and their graphical structures. By integrating the principles of graph theory into neural networks, GNNs leverage existing network patterns to enhance predictive capabilities for medical and scientific entities. This piece also explores the applications of graph learning in medicine and biology, offering insights into how they can inform scientific discoveries and clinical decision-making processes.

Significant advancements in measuring very weak luminosity from accreting white dwarfs have enabled novel constraints to be imposed on certain theoretical models. In this research, we investigate the possibility of inelastic dark matter being converted into a stable particle through interaction with nuclear nuclei, a process that could occur if the particle has a non-zero spin. Our analysis reveals that the nuclear reaction rate would vary based on the target's composition, allowing us to establish more rigorous limitations on this particle mass, specifically between 0.1 GeV and 10 GeV, depending on the setup and model. Furthermore, we discover that the spin-dependent interaction between nuclei and particles consisting of a heavy fourth-generation fermion, with a mass greater than 50 GeV, could be limited to less than $10^{-32}$ cm$^2$ cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$ solar L$_{\odot}$ in certain circumstances. In another model scenario, involving an extra U(1) gauge boson from a left-right symmetric theory, with very small coupling constants, our analysis shows that the rate of conversion between matter and the boson is limited to less than $10^{-10}$ times the predicted standard model rate, thereby imposing significant constraints on this type of model.

Advancements in technological capabilities have enabled sharing sensitive data over digital platforms, prompting the need for data protection measures. Graph data poses unique challenges for privacy preservation due to interconnections between data points. While preserving the utility of interdependent relationships, researchers have proposed multiple strategies to maintain confidentiality. However, selecting the most effective approach remains complex due to various content characteristics. This study introduces a graph privacy consultant that evaluates multiple content properties and recommends the most suitable privacy-preserving technique, testing its reliability and efficiency on diverse synthetic and real-world graphs.

This paper explores the feasibility and implications of hiding a pure concealed sector, as discussed in Arxiv:2203:00973 and arXiv:1810:01640. We propose a new framework to analyze these models and compare them to the visible sector, examining the purity, hiding, and detection capabilities of the confined $\mathbb{Z}_2$-odd states. We examine the possibilities of both solid and liquid phases in the early universe and investigate the possibility of a third neutrino flavor, considering the significant effects on neutrino oscillations. We also discuss the potential of detecting this hidden flavor through a unique, flavor-dependent decay of $Z$ boson.

This study compares fragmentation patterns of light-quark and gluon jets within $pp$ and Pb+Pb collisions at a centre-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. Using a template-jet method, we measure the fragmentation functions in light-quark and gluon jets in single-particle spectra covering $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ from 20 to 1500 GeV and rapidity $|y| < 0.9$. We observe that in both proton-proton and lead-lead collisions, the fragmentation patterns exhibit the same relative fragmentation behaviour for light-quark and gluon jets. Furthermore, we find that in lead-lead collisions, the overall jet fragmentation shifts towards higher fractions of total jet $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ compared to proton-proton collisions. The results are presented in the context of parton shower and medium interactions.

The CP2K program package, often listed among top scientific applications, excels in hybrid density functional theory and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics simulations. With advancements in high-performance computing infrastructure, recent developments such as multi-threaded linear scaling methods and active electrons techniques have enabled the use of larger systems on more affordable machines. However, the road to exascale computing presents new challenges and opportunities, particularly with the need for better linear algebra libraries and software frameworks for portable, efficient simulations. Our latest research highlights recent breakthroughs in CP2K's computational methods and their success on the world's most powerful supercomputers, paving the way for exploring the path to exascale computing.

We present novel observations from the Focus Optical Spectrograph for Imaging the Sun's Ionosphere (FOXSI) instrument, which detected hard X-rays emitted during the dynamic period on December 13, 2021. This subflare was driven by a significant magnetic reconnection event that caused two bright regions of plasma to merge. Unusually, these sources did not separate as typically expected in solar flares. Our analysis reveals that these X-rays were the dimmest ever recorded by FOXSI, corresponding to count rates of 0.05-0.1 counts per second per pixel. This corresponds to very low X-ray flux levels, around 10^-3 to 10^-2 times the typical levels seen in flares. This is the first time that such low-count-rate HXR emissions have been detected by FOXSI, and we discuss the challenges these present in confirming the presence of thermal and non-thermal components within these X-rays.

Predicting social impact from visual content such as images, videos, and text is an area of significant interest to law enforcement agencies, enabling them to prevent violent acts and reduce harm. A variety of deep learning approaches, including those based on images, audio, and social media text, have been developed to this end. However, there is a notable absence of visual-based methods for predicting social violence within a spatial context. This paper aims to fill this gap by introducing SocIAI (Social Impact Assessment with Image classification), a system designed to predict harmful content within geographical regions by analyzing photographs. SocIAI leverages graph neural networks (GNNs) to analyze the interconnected social media data, taking into consideration the location, coordinates, and timestamp. To address the issue of uneven distribution and limited data availability, SocIAI employs a technique of augmenting graph node durations. Furthermore, it addresses the problem of overfitting during training by analyzing node importance, and proposes a method to enhance generalization by randomly extending node durations. Using two distinct social violence indicators, SocIAI achieves exceptional performance in predicting impact within unseen geographical regions.

The dimension of the conformal field theory's representation, particularly its ground state, corresponds to the solution of the Euler Arnold equations for the su2 algebra. The logarithm of this dimension, known as the entanglement/Euler number, can be expressed as an infinite sum involving powers of the inverse cutoff. When evaluated numerically for a specific cutoff value, this entanglement/Euler number, denoted as E, correlates strongly with another parameter denoted as rho. As a result, a one-dimensional function exists that explains the observed data trends, despite the existence of complex dynamics in the Euler Arnold equation.

This research introduces a novel optimal method for determining the position and range of an object using multiple sensors, with each sensor measuring its distance to the object. We assume the objects being tracked do not deviate from the plane perpendicular to each sensor's axis, which is typical for acoustic beamforming with short arrays. This array perpendicularity assumption simplifies the problem and can be resolved analytically. Our proposed method employs an efficient optimization technique based on completing the square to solve the object's position estimation problem, resulting in closed-form estimates of position and variance that do not require complex numerical methods. Additionally, this solution allows us to identify the optimal sensor configuration and is adaptable to various beamforming techniques.

Researchers are investigating the hidden sectors of the universe, particularly in light of recent findings from LHC and other experiments, which hint at the existence of phenomena beyond the Standard Model. Our hypothesis involves a concealed sector that decouples from the visible universe following an early separation and subsequent recombination. This process leads to the creation of multiple universes, which are characterized by distinct temperatures and thermal histories, and ultimately results in the observable universe as we know it. A simplified model illustrates the concept's feasibility and predicts hidden sector features such as dark matter composition and production mechanisms stemming from the universe decoupling and recombination. This is further supported by numerical simulations of the universe's thermal development and its impact on hidden sector constitutents.

A comprehensive search for same-sign W boson pairs generated through processes other than collision is presented, utilizing proton-proton collision data collected at a 13 TeV energy level, with a total of 0.59 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity, acquired by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Observations align closely with theoretical expectations concerning the presence of two charged W bosons and no neutral W boson in the final state, with lepton decays exhibited and substantial evidence suggesting the presence of electroweak production processes dominating over the previously recorded rare strong force-mediated occurrence. In the final state featuring two same-sign leptons, two jets, and minimal missing transverse momentum, observables match the predictions regarding the presence of two charged W bosons and no neutral W boson. This alignment is consistent with the expectations concerning the electroweak production process. A new mathematical model of the electroweak generation process involving fourth-generation fermions and the charged Goldstone boson of the standard model is introduced, with the findings agreeing well with the model.

This work tackles the challenge of enhancing color information in monochromatic images captured by cameras with distinct color filters. Existing color translation approaches are limited to specific camera systems and fail to adapt to different ones due to substantial visual differences. Our solution involves embedding domain translation within a deep neural network that recovers color information from grayscale images. By leveraging features from monochromatic images and incorporating prior color information with self-supervised learning, we can effectively adapt to various camera systems without requiring extensive dataset collection or precise metadata. Our method is demonstrated to yield accurate colorization and illumination improvements, yielding significant gains in visual quality and efficiency compared to existing methods.

Utilizing a novel mathematical representation for the curvature term in Friedmann's equation, we develop an approach that allows us to assess spatial curvature's impact without interference from dust, radiation, or dark energy influence. This model's analysis, based on four independent datasets of spatial distance measurements, reveals that these data support a flat universe but support increased curvature than the $\Lambda$CDM model predicts. Notably, the curvature's impact on this framework is significant, estimated at a $3\sigma$ level. Furthermore, our method is not constrained by potential problems associated with alternative models that describe the universe's energy composition.

The widespread reliance on outdated versions of software files in development projects is a prevalent issue. Although file copies are common in such scenarios, there has been a lack of research exploring how developers effectively manage these duplicates. We present MetaMaint, an automated tool that tackles this problem by detecting and managing entire project repositories on GitHub, rather than focusing solely on individual files. By analyzing the repository as a whole, MetaMaint identifies files requiring deletion, regardless of their location, and proposes valuable insights into the evolution of the repository over time. Our analysis reveals that addressing file copies could lead to significant improvements in repository health and maintenance.

The eclipsing binary BD And has been the subject of debate, with observations conflicting and challenging its proposed status as a pair of stars with varying periods. The discovery of a candidate Gamma Doradus variability in BD And has been found and confirmed using data from the TESS mission. Analysis using the TESS light curve and other data suggests that the BD And system consists of multiple components, including a third body, and that the observed eclipses are consistent with a binary system with specific star sizes and densities. The consensus is that the BD And system is composed of stars with periods matching that of the TESS data and that any previously proposed fourth member is unnecessary to explain the observed variability. The stars in BD And have been found to have masses and radii consistent with typical BD And system parameters, with the consensus being that BD And is best described as a binary system with periods matching that of the TESS data.
This paper has more content in its forward and backend sections.

Cross-domain recommendation has the potential to tackle the challenge of sparse training data, yet current methods are hindered by the limitations of their collaborative signal learning in co-expressed item spaces and their reliance on item embeddings for representation. These approaches fail to capture comprehensive attribute-based preferences, especially when co-expressed items are not available in other domains. To address these shortcomings, our proposed solution involves rethinking the collaboration process by sharing domain-specific latent spaces and their sparse properties to preserve precise user preference learning in isolated, domain-specific latent spaces. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of incorporating comprehensive attribute preferences by mapping items to these preferences and sharing them across domains to facilitate collaborative learning. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing recommendation accuracy and generalization capabilities when sparse data is available.

We establish deformation theories for perpendicular bundles and symplectic bundles, proving that the deformations of these bundles respect their respective bundle constraints. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the deformations of perpendicular bundles can be correspondingly mapped to the deformations of their associated symplectic bundles, given a fixed structure group.

Let P_n be the set of all partitions of a positive integer n into parts of various sizes. We define D_{<k}(n) as the subset of partitions in P_n that use each size at most k-1 times. Let C_l be the set of all distinct sub-partitions (components) with sizes less than k across all partitions in D_{<k}(n). We aim to find J_x, the count of distinct sub-partitions containing a specific integer x in C_l.

This research examines the reliability of least squares estimation under simultaneous biases in features and outcomes across multiple samples. It establishes error bounds for standard LS methods and a more advanced alternative, showing that even bias across samples can be compensated for, leading to consistent model learning similar to the fully accurate conditions. Our findings also indicate that the additional regression achieved by reliable LS methods comes at a notable cost in terms of efficiency. To address this trade-off, we explore two approaches: minimizing the impact of uncertainty using our novel 'projection adversarial training' or leveraging outcome uncertainty information through 'Bayesian posterior mean estimation'. The latter approach outperforms the more complex projection adversarial method when uncertainty can be determined, and our experiments validate these developments.

This presentation discusses the recent progress and research updates at the LHC concerning J/ψ, ψ(2S), B mesons, X(3872), Y(3872), and other X,Y,Z states. Research at the LHCb experiment is focused on the formation and properties of these unusual states. In addition, analyses at ATLAS and CMS experiments are presented, focusing the LHC's potential contributions to our understanding of these enigmatic particles

Within the disordered Hubbard model, we investigate how disorder impacts quantum critical phenomena, utilizing both numerical findings and analytical arguments. It is demonstrated through numerical evidence that dissorder can lead to the separation of the lower and upper parts of the density of states already present in the non-interacting system ($U=0$). By employing an analytical approach, we investigate the implications of this disorder-induced split, and identify that it can give rise to singular exponent behavior, which contrasts with the universal behavior of the non-disordered Kondo lattice model. We observe that these exponents change gradually with disorder level, but certain attributes, such as power-law decay in density of states below the Fermi energy, do not disappear completely. The obtained results can be described through a real-space renormalization group based on the singlet formation process, which is illustrated through numerical data. This method also allows for the investigation of other quantities, such as the shortest singlet length, which is found to decrease significantly with increased disorder level.

The set of Coxeter elements in a Coxeter group, particularly in the type $A_{n-1}$, possesses a distinctive characteristic: it is the unique minimal set among all conjugates with respect to the length of the elements. Research has shown that this property holds true for the extended $A_{n}$ Coxeter group as well, including the Coxeter group of the Dynkin diagram $A_{n}^{(1)}$. In a study involving the finite $A_{n}$ Coxeter group, the length of elements within each conjugate class has been explored, utilizing this research, a new proof for the foundation theorem of the $A_{n}$ Coxeter group, distinct from the previously established proof, has been established. Furthermore, the nature of the length of the Coxeter elements has been confirmed, acting as a key factor in the alternative proof of the foundation theorem.

Solitons in interacting scalar field theories, when there's no $SO(2)$ invariance, were previously deemed impossible based on an old argument. However, we discovered that such solitons can actually exist within the broader context of non-$SO(2)$ invariant theories. We constructed a specific model that supports both stable particle solitons and reflective domain walls. This discovery has significant implications for various fields, including inflationary cosmology, where the universe may be part of a higher-dimensional space that includes field theories lacking $SO(2)$ invariance. It's also possible that some of the dark matter we observe today consists of these stable particle solitons.

We introduce a novel Bayesian framework that draws inspiration from the structure of human learning. This framework is specifically designed to address the inverse reinforcement learning problem under the condition that agents cannot access complete control over their environment. Building upon a partial regulation model proposed by a previous study, our work introduces a two-level hierarchical structure that mimics the relationship between a child and a teacher. At the upper level, our model employs a hierarchical Bayesian approach to capture a teacher's strategy in guiding an agent, focusing on the aspects of when and how an teacher provides assistance. At the data collection point, our model utilizes trajectory data generated during a teaching process to infer critical parameters of our model. These parameters enable our model to infer further details regarding an agent's intended objectives, as well as when and how an agent's teacher provides assistance. Experimental validation using simulated and real-world datasets has validated the effectiveness of our model.

This study robustly examines the transfer regions associated with small loops near punctures on surfaces, focusing on their relationship with specific subgroups of the surface's fundamental group. We determine which subgroups of index $k$ contain minimal normal subgroups and demonstrate that only subgroups of index $k \le 7$ can do so. From this point forward, we restrict our analysis to prime indices $k$. Utilizing our findings, we prove the existence of at least one transfer region for each subgroup of prime index $k$ on any surface, provided $k$ is not a Fanashev index. Additionally, we show that these regions vary continuously with the surface metric under certain conditions. Our work also involves exploring the connection between the robust transfer regions and the minimal normal subgroups within them, revealing that only subgroups of index $k \le 5$ have open regions consisting entirely of normal subgroups. Lastly, we relate the robust transfer regions to the coverings of surface bundles over the disk, showing that at least one robust transfer region exists for each Galois cover of the surface.

Using deep reinforcement learning, autonomous control of mobile robots is becoming more feasible, 
however, several intricate control problems remain a significant challenge. 
In our research, two distinct complex control issues are identified: controlling a robot under uncertain conditions and managing underactuated control. 
A novel strategy is proposed to tackle these challenges through the application of a dual-staged deep reinforcement learning framework. 
This new framework is specifically designed to take into account control limitations when dealing with uncertainty and control constraints in the presence of underactuation. 
It is demonstrated that our approach is more effective than conventional deep reinforcement learning methods in addressing these challenging control scenarios. 
Successful implementations of our method are shown to control a mobile robot despite the presence of uncertainty and manage underactuated control.

This study investigates the mass distribution of black holes over time, focusing on two main growth patterns and the development of very heavy black holes. By the present day, massive black holes with masses greater than 10 to the power of 8 solar masses have been observed throughout the universe and in particular, supermassive black holes with masses greater than 10 to the power of 9 solar masses have been found at the center of galaxies. The research found that the majority of heavy black holes developed through continuous growth, with the exception of the smallest and smallest of these, which have unique distributions. These findings highlight the complex and diverse ways in which black holes grow and the need to understand the heavy seed growth model, which plays a key role in the mass distribution of black holes over time. By taking into account the growth of black holes that occur at high redshifts, the study offers a more comprehensive and accurate model for the mass distribution of black holes over time, and the evolution of galaxies.

Advancements in high-throughput automated analysis using machine learning have transformed scientific data processing. Nevertheless, current applications often fall short of transparency and reproducibility standards needed in scientific research. To rectify this challenge, this study presents a modular neural network that accurately fits inelastic neutron scattering spectra. The framework incorporates a calibrated output layer, enabling precise calculation of chi-squared statistics. This innovative approach quantifies the discrepancy between observed data and theoretical predictions. Furthermore, gradient-based optimization methods can differentiate through the neural network, facilitating precise quantification. The method's effectiveness and reliability have been validated using both simulated and real-world neutron scattering data. Notably, our analysis confirms that our approach yields accurate results even when data quality is compromised by realistic factors such as limited counting statistics and readout errors.

Advancements in computer technology have enabled the global sharing of preprints--unreviewed publications hosted online.  Although the concept dates back to the 1970s, preprints have only recently gained widespread adoption within the scientific community.  This article examines the historical development of prepublication services over the past three decades, highlighting key milestones and the eventual establishment of preprints as a vital component of scholarly publication.  The study provides an in-depth analysis of the growing preprint ecosystem, exploring its impact on various stakeholders and different disciplines, while also considering potential future trends.  The findings suggest that authors who engage with preprints receive enhanced professional exposure and increased citation rates, institutions with established preprint programs experience improved publication outcomes, and disciplines utilizing preprints exhibit accelerated publication velocities, all at reduced costs.

This work presents a digital laboratory journal that can be accessed from any device with internet connectivity. Through this journal, researchers can systematically compile and analyze laboratory data in a progressive manner, starting with the selection of the appropriate experiment template, which facilitates accurate and consistent record-keeping. In the journal's initial entry section, essential information such as the experiment type, participants, assistants, and date is systematically captured. Furthermore, all procedural and observational details can be documented in a structured format, which can be seamlessly exported in various formats, including PDF and CSV. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed digital laboratory journal, we conducted real-life tests in our physics and microbiology departments and analyzed the results. Our findings indicate that the journal significantly enhances and streamlines data management, which in turn increases the reliability of our laboratory's records. Ultimately, the streamlined export process enables efficient and effective reporting of our experiment findings.

High-entropy alloys, comprising multiple principal elements, exhibit unusual structures and exceptional performance characteristics, excelling in exceptional toughness and resilience. The complex nature of HEAs poses significant challenges in understanding the element interactions and predicting their behavior. Emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and big data analysis present new opportunities to overcome these obstacles. This work delves into the potential of machine learning in investigating HEAs, highlighting its advantages and benefits. Additionally, we explore the use of evolutionary algorithms in optimizing design, as well as challenges associated with HEA research, such as data scarcity and the element's impact on thermodynamic calculations. The element Sc's impact on thermodynamic predictions is explored in detail, and future prospects for the field are discussed.

The possibility of $L=1$ composite partner decays into a $D^{\ast}D\pi$ final state is investigated.
We determine the production rate of these decays using the light-front projection method to connect the wave functions of the $D^{\ast}$, $D$, $\pi$, and $T_{cc}^+$ particles.
Calculations reveal that the decay rates exhibit significant sensitivity to the choice of monomial type in the light-front projection.
Additionally, the form of the monomial type also affects decay widths for heavy quark decays like $B_c \to J/\psi\pi$ and $D_s \to K D^{\ast}$.
These findings suggest the need for direct experimental measurement of $T_{cc}^+$ related production and decay data.
Ultimately, such studies may help resolve the issue of light-front projection scheme dependence.

Machine learning models with predefined parameters can benefit from defining a set of possible outcomes, which we refer to as the latent state space. This concept applies across various domains, including graphical neural networks and the dynamics of differential equations. Our goal is to create a unified approach to defining the probabilistic outcome pool for defining these models' latent spaces, by defining the rate of transition between different states in the latent space as the result of a differential equation or random chance. This unified approach enables the use of current graphical neural networks and defines the latent state space in a manner that accommodates various types of latent variable models, such as those defined by differential equations and probabilistic models with a set of possible states. Our method enables the implicit definition of the latent space without explicitly defining its structure. This approach enables the efficient training of graphical neural networks using current optimization techniques and defines the latent state space in a manner that accommodates various types of models, such as those defined by differential equations and chance-based models.

This work establishes a criterion for the nonlinearity distance of mappings from $\mathbb{F}^n$ to $\mathbb{F}^m$ and uses it to determine lower bounds for the nonlinearity of first-order derivative non-linear mappings from a finite field to another finite field, leveraging Sidon sets defined over these fields. Specifically, our results show the nonlinearity lower bounds for $F:x\mapsto dx^p$ and $F:x\mapsto x^p+Ax+B$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ and $F:x\mapsto x^{p}+Ax^{l}+B$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$. Binarized matrices with all row and column sums equal to $d$ are represented by a unique pair of binary vectors called 'Non-Uniform Coded Data', which have specific values of 0 and 1 throughout their lengths. Binarized matrices constructed using these vectors from the set $\{0,1\}^n$ have 1s in each cell and at least one 0 in each row and column. We present a novel sampling method that randomly selects pairs of 'Non-Uniform Coded Data' matrices from the set $\{0,1\}^n$ and then calculates the total number of 1s in each row and column. The sampled matrices will have fixed margins if and only if each element in the pair is marginally balanced. The sampling method's efficiency is explored based on the common margin $d$. The probability of achieving balanced margins for both matrices is highest when the margin is approximately half the length of the vectors ($\frac{n}{2}$). The probability drops significantly when the margin is significantly less or greater than this value. The time it takes for the sampler to produce a uniformly random matrix and the expected size of the matrices in the pair are studied in detail in relation to the margin $d$. Precision in measuring differential cross sections is crucial for constraining current parton distribution function models, yet existing cross section models are plagued by substantial uncertainties, especially at low $x$ and low $Q^2$ values. As LHC and non-leptonic weak interaction experiments generate vast amounts of high-precision data, parton distribution function uncertainties are becoming a major limitation in interpreting these findings. To overcome this issue, global parton distribution function fits are being revised to incorporate all data and minimize biases, with new frameworks such as the RT-Framework facilitating this process by incorporating user-friendly parts of the RTM framework.

This document highlights the recent release of version 0.7.5 for the HeiDL (Artificial Intelligence and Data Analysis toolkit), a primary maintenance focus being the integration of user feedback and continuous improvement of key functionalities including clustering, outlier detection, manifold learning, and information retrieval. In addition to updating the toolkit's open-source components and user-friendly interface options, significant internal enhancements have been made to enhance unit testing, code documentation, and overall maintainability of the software library. Furthermore, the paper discusses the development of an extensive manual now available on the project's wiki platform to support new-comers to the toolkit. Finally, the paper provides an update on the latest research breakthroughs achieved using data and analysis tools within the toolkit's framework, complete with the necessary code for reproducibility now hosted on the project's GitHub repository.

A new technique has been developed to rapidly create optical frequency grids by detecting resonances in an accelerated microresonator while changing its tuning rate. This method, which uses a simple detector, can produce grid outcomes comparable to those achieved by more complex feedback methods, but with the added benefit of being able to identify new resonances as they emerge. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique by successfully creating and locking a grid of 500 lasers.
