The accurate mass-to-charge ratios obtained through this method contribute to a better understanding of nuclear structure and reactions in regions far from stability.

This detailed document serves as a precise introduction to standardizing flows in lattice field theory, targeting lattice physicists unfamiliar with the concept. It explains the principles of flow equations, identifies flow-fixed points, and explores the criteria distinguishing effective flow directions. The document also explores the connection between standardizing flows and renormalization group trajectories in theory spaces. We examine various lattice field theories as practical examples, including quasi-free theories that model free theories on curved lattices, $O(N)$ models representing interacting scalar fields, and lattice gauge theories. This comprehensive tutorial is particularly relevant to the development of lattice effective field theories and the exploration of theory spaces.

Named Entity Recognition through recognition accuracy is an important aspect of optical recognition but has been limited by recognition accuracy, particularly for recognition of text that adheres to a specific pattern defined by a regular expression. We investigate the effectiveness of taking into account the structure of text through a regular expression during training to improve recognition accuracy of such text. By developing a novel method that enhances the recognition accuracy of text that fits a specific pattern defined by a regular expression, we demonstrate its effectiveness on an optical recognition dataset of phone numbers. The approach involves only a one-time transformation of the model derived from a specific method and does not necessitate any alterations to the model's architecture or training procedure. The results show that considering the text structure defined by a regular expression can enhance the recognition accuracy of such text significantly.

This research investigates the production of top quarks through proton-nucleus collisions at the Fixed Target top quark factory. We examine the top quark, top antiquon pair and single top quon generations, focusing on the top quon distribution functions in nuclei and comparing proton and nucleus results. Our analysis considers top quark pair and single top quon correlations, as well as kinematic characteristics such as rapidity and rapidity distributions. We also explore the proton-nucleon asymmetry for various processes and quark top quark or single top quon reactions, with these findings showing clear distinctions from those of proton-proton collisions.

This work focuses on text-to-SQL linguistic analysis through end-to-end models with auxiliary tasks that facilitate automatic generation of SQL queries from natural language statements. The proposed models cover various stages of text-to-SQL linguistic analysis, including entity recognition, SQL parsing, and data type mapping. An innovative auxiliary task has been designed to guide these models towards generating more accurate outputs. Experimental results on two cross-domain datasets, comprising text-to-SQL tasks from disparate domains, demonstrate the efficacy of these models in adapting to new domains with limited or no domain-specific training data.

The frequency range of 110-162 MHz in the LoTSS DR1 survey affected survey area coverage and resulted in a sample of 55,531 galaxies within that area, having an absolute magnitude range of -11.54 to -3.76. These were then used to create galaxy samples at various areas of the sky, allowing researchers to examine galaxy number density variation with mass for galaxies with absolute magnitudes ranging from -11.54 to -9.66. A discovered relationship between galaxy density and absolute magnitude showed that higher mass galaxies tend to have a greater distance from the origin in data, with potential sources of error being found at both low and high mass. A detected galaxy bias pattern, where more massive galaxies exhibit a greater degree of deviation, was observed across multiple extragalactic probes. This study presents the first examination of galaxy energy distribution and characteristics in the magnitude range of -11.54 to -13.54, specifically within the area of the sky not yet fully explored by LoTSS, providing significant implications for theoretical models of galaxy evolution.

This study introduces a novel, efficient algorithm resolving a critical challenge in high-dimensional machine learning known as the High-Dimensional Ranking Problem. By incorporating an L1-regularization term into the Pinark loss function, we formulate the High-Dimensional Ranking Lasso Problem. To address this issue, we develop an adaptive-sieving approach coupled with proximal operator calculations. Our algorithm's asymptotic convergence has been rigorously proven, and experimentally, it exhibits exceptional performance in comparing various alternatives.

As knowledge of large-scale systems grows, understanding the entropy generation of these systems remains a notable knowledge gap. We successfully measured the specific rate of entropy generation in a microsystem over various temporal and dynamical ranges. We utilized an optical microtrapper for microparticles for these measurements and developed an effective method for extracting the reversible and dissipative displacement components. The observed entropy generation exhibits a distinctly convex shape for both slow and weak variations as well as in-scenario weak-coupling and adiabatic limits within rapid quenching. This understanding supports the hypothesis that entropy generation follows universal laws, even at large scales, and may be influenced by system dynamics and time scales, rather than just number of microstates.

This letter introduces a novel paradigm of AI-enabled ecology, aiming to compensate for current and past ecological damage caused by technological advancement and economic development. We acknowledge the potential hidden environmental costs associated with AI-driven ecology and propose a comprehensive evaluation framework to reveal the ecological implications of AI applications throughout their lifecycle. By unveiling these hidden costs, our framework seeks to accelerate the development of truly sustainable AI solutions, ensuring they do not exacerbate ecological harm.

Research on prescriptive procedure monitoring has progressed significantly in the last two decades, focusing on 1) the psychological aspects, 2) the governing principles, and 3) the beneficial effects. These aspects have been extensively researched within the realms of cognitive psychology, organizational psychology, and management science respectively. Despite these advancements, the monitoring research community still lacks clarity on several key questions. This article reviews the current uncertainties in monitoring research and outlines potential directions for future inquiry, thereby providing a springboard for further study.

This study investigates the identification of optimal control parameters in the generalized Boussinesq model, which models viscous, heat-gaining fluids. These parameters influence crucial heat transfer properties and are critical for achieving desired temperature distributions. Such models find applications in various industrial processes, including polymer heating and metal glass production. Due to the nonlinear and convective nature of the model, traditional numerical methods can become computationally expensive. This research employs an alternative approach, utilizing an approximate solution and cost function derivative approximations along with the adjoint variable. This approach allows for the efficient determination of the control parameter that minimizes the cost function. Two examples demonstrate the method's capability to generate a desired temperature distribution and a specific Biot number across the domain.

Building predictive models is often complicated by the limitations and diverse characteristics of various machine learning algorithms. Combining multiple models can enhance predictive performance, but evaluating and selecting stacking combinations presents a significant challenge. Our research focuses on the issue of data redundancy in stacking, where certain training samples contribute negligibly to model construction and can be discarded to optimize the process. We developed a new technique for addressing this problem, focusing on stacking regression tasks, and demonstrated its effectiveness through experiments on synthetic data and six real-world datasets using various stacking algorithm combinations. The results show that applying our method leads to substantial reductions in computation time, specifically a 90% decrease for one combination in the synthetic dataset example, and similar significant gains for other algorithms and datasets.

In studies of opinion models based on social networks, the assumption is often made that agents' connections remain stable over time. However, this assumption may be flawed, as the preference for interacting with certain connected agents can change due to influences from their connected agents. When opinion models incorporate this preferential behavior, the agents' social networks evolve in a dynamic way, making the system harder to analyze due to its stability challenges. To understand how opinion models with preferable interactions behave over time, this research examines how opinions and preferred social networks evolve concurrently. Through the analysis, the research reveals that starting from preferred separation, agents gradually move towards a stable state where they only interact with agents whose preferences for interacting with them are 100%. However, at this stable social network state, the agents' opinions may become extremely diverse, essentially random, resulting in a significant increase in the variability of how opinions stabilize relative to traditional opinion models assuming stable social networks.

Recently, a new type of object called 'hairy black stars' has been proposed, featuring supersymmetric configurations with charges in type IIB supergravity. These configurations consist of strings with specific properties that match the properties of D1 and D5 charges. The objects consist of strings looped around the equator of the sphere $S^2$, embedded in the $S^5$ part of the background. Research has found that when the loops contract, they lead to the breakdown of the near-horizon approximation and modify the topology of the horizon. In this paper, we explore the properties of these contractions, analyze the change in the horizon's topology, and utilize a scalar field to estimate the mass of these objects. Our analysis shows that the mass decreases as the loops contract, ultimately resulting in a significant drop in mass when fully contracted.

Comparing mRNA transcription rates to protein synthesis data often shows
evidence of transcriptional delay across both prokaryotes and eukaryotes,
likely a result of RNA processing and transcription dynamics. To accurately
model these patterns and reveal delayed transcription trends in RNA-seq data,
we developed the Fitted Integral Model (FIM), which accounts for RNA processing
properties. Application of FIM to RNA-seq datasets from diverse organisms
revealed typical transcriptional delay durations of 4-10 minutes, consistent with
prevailing models of RNA processing. Analyzing correlations between delay and
mRNA features suggests extended transcription periods for genes producing pre-mRNAs.
Furthermore, simulation of RNA-seq data with FIM confirms that these modeling
results accurately reflect the underlying delayed transcription trends in prokaryotic
and eukaryotic genomes.

In even-proton, even-neutron nuclei near N=Z at low angular momentum levels, there is an unusual situation where multiple nuclear ground state configurations can coexist. Traditionally, the tensor force has been seen as the primary driver of high-spin ground states but its effect on low-angular-momentum states is less clear. Our study reveals that the tensor force also plays a pivotal role in high-spin states of $^{64}$Ni, specifically the high-spin state at spin 4, and that this phenomenon is due to the interaction between a proton in a high-orbital and the neutron pairs supporting it.

Chiral theories, which have a property called anomaly, can serve as a platform to investigate the relationship between dual theories, which are equivalent through duality. Theories with SU(N) symmetry and constituents consisting of fermions called quarks exhibit two types of dynamics: one where they become weakly interactive at low energies for odd values of N and another with gauge invariance loss for even values of N. By assigning specific charges to the quarks in these models, the resulting dual descriptions for the low-energy SU(N) model with monochromatic interactions and the loss of gauge invariance in the bichirmon interactions can be found to share identical properties. The findings suggest that these two low-energy models may have the same characteristics.

A linear complementary set of group codes (LCGC) over a finite principal ideal field F consists of a series of group codes whose direct sum spans the entire space of the field. Researchers pioneered the concept of LGC over Galois fields and subsequent applications over chain rings and principal ideal domains. In this research, criteria for LGC over finite principal ideal fields have been established and demonstrated through specific polynomial circulant codes. Additionally, group codes with known parameters over a finite principal ideal field and their corresponding LGC have been identified and analyzed.

Exact inference in graphical models, specifically through the max-product elimination (MPE) algorithm, is crucial for solving complex optimization problems under constraints. However, traditional approaches can be hindered by a lack of feasible solutions. While Lagrange multipliers and projected optimization methods address constraints, they often require complex implementations and dependencies on external tools. Our work presents a straightforward, graph-based method to integrate constraints into MPE, enhancing its reliability and convergence under various conditions. This novel approach efficiently implements key methods, such as Lagrange duality and dual ascent, directly within the graph factor representation framework.

Many everyday actions we perform rely on complex sensor systems that detect the presence or absence of objects. One critical aspect of this coordination is identifying when an object is unexpectedly missing. Although humans effectively utilize visual and auditory cues for this purpose, current sensor systems are limited to processing one type of cue at a time. To overcome these limitations, we propose an advanced dropped object detection system that synchronizes asynchronous visual and audio inputs. By leveraging deep learning techniques to align visual and audio data temporally and spatially, our method achieves superior performance on the DROPOBJECT dataset compared to existing methods that process visual and audio information separately.

We investigate shear thickening transitions in dense particle suspensions under rapid deformation. These suspensions demonstrate a phase transition characterized by distinct fluid and shear thickened states, with coexisting states observed at the critical point. Analysis of stress correlation functions and dynamic structure factors across multiple experiments and deformations reveals universal scaling behaviors. These scaling relationships allow us to collapse data into simplified forms, providing clear insights into the dynamics of the thickening transitions and establishing a framework for future studies of similar physical systems.

This research aims to address the challenge of accurately forecasting electricity consumption patterns on an hourly basis. Several traditional and advanced statistical methods, including AR, ARIMA, ARIMA-NET, ARIMAX, and exponential smoothing models, are evaluated and compared. Data covering the years 2017 to 2020 is analyzed, with notable disruptions observed in March 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, prompting the selection of March 2020 as the testing phase. Results demonstrate the superior performance of the ARIMAX model, incorporating meteorological variables, in providing precise hour-by-hour demand estimates.

Over the last 15 years, Google Web search has allowed users to personalize their results based on their past search history, enabling more tailored outcomes.  However, this customization can also cause users to miss out on relevant information by sticking to results similar to what they have seen before, essentially creating an information loop that reinforces their existing habits and biases.  This phenomenon can cause users to fail to notice new and important information, ultimately hindering their ability to learn from their past mistakes.  This effect has been tested through a controlled study using Google's typical search results and has been observed to cause participants to deliberately avoid certain topics by choosing searches based on their history, even when those topics were relevant to the task at hand, ultimately causing the typical reliance on past search history to negatively affect the task outcomes.

Program synthesis is the process of automatically generating correct programs
from specified specifications.  Current program synthesis methods using Natural
Language Processing and Software Engineering techniques struggle to produce complex
programs, particularly those requiring control structures like loops and conditionals.
To address this limitation, we propose a novel deep learning approach that leverages
Visual Basic and Flowcharts to synthesize loop-containing programs in natural languages.
By training a neural network on graphs representing Flowcharts, our method synthesizes
programs matching the structural patterns learned from training data.  Experimental results
show our graph-based approach outperforms traditional methods in program synthesis tasks.

Diminution techniques in climate modeling involve reducing the computational load by limiting spatial resolution, temporal frequency, or geographic scope. Given the inherently complex and costly nature of climate simulations, a wide range of techniques employing diminution strategies have been developed and applied across climate dynamics and other computational fields. This review outlines various diminution methods utilized in climate modeling, highlighting their underlying principles and associated benefits and limitations. Specifically, each technique's impact on spatial, temporal, and geographic aspects is examined, followed by a discussion of resolution reduction methods and their associated challenges. Ultimately, the future prospects of diminution techniques in climate prediction are explored.

The relativistic atomic composition of specific Os isoelectronic sequence lines has been determined, specifically the ion states of Os through Au and the MII through W higher charged ions.  This research involved calculating accurate atomic composition for each ion state at relevant ejecta opacity temperatures, with the result that the four lowest charged ion states dominate the opacity calculations.  This research, along with other data, enables more precise modeling of kilonova ejecta opacity contributions.  Data, including the atomic composition and emission/absorption coefficients, are being released for use in informing ejecta opacity and photon diffusion time in kilonova models.

Radiation therapy targeting abdominal malignancies relies on precise volumetric assessment of mobile organs like the stomach and small bowel. These organs' mobility necessitates restricted treatment zones to minimize exposure to healthy tissue and thereby reduce potential side effects. The application of radiation fields guided by organ motion data, known as motion management, is essential but relies on accurate segmentation. A recent study presented an automated, annotation-free deep learning approach for segmenting the gastrointestinal tract on CT scans, allowing clinicians to establish and apply segmentations across multiple patients with minimal manual input. The model's performance showed superior results when evaluated against conventional image processing techniques and a traditional machine learning algorithm, with promising clinical applicability for streamlining treatment planning and execution.

This study introduces a systematic approach for examining how different aspects of composition influence outcome predictions. The methodology employs linear mathematical concepts and visualizes results to facilitate meaningful visual assessments of compositional effects on predictions.

A comprehensive analysis of 113 exoplanets with masses less than 100 Earth masses, discovered via the CORALIE and/or HARPS spectrographs, reveals the absence of plancts in the range between 20 and 200 Earth masses. The detection efficiency's dependence on distance and planet mass indicates that the absent region may be due to an inherent feature in the mass distribution of exoplanets, potentially involving a transformation of gas-rich planets in the sub-Saturn mass range into hot Neptunes rather than the mere under-sampling effect.

Stable dark matter that interacts through a scalar or pseudoscalar mediator could significantly alter galaxy formation, as it compresses the dark matter distribution function in phase space. This property might resolve discrepancies between observed galaxy characteristics and those predicted by standard cold dark matter models. By considering a scenario where dark matter couples to a scalar pseudoscalar state like the axion, we find that galaxy counts data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey already impose constraints on the dark matter's velocity distribution. These constraints will likely grow tighter with an expanding dataset, potentially reaching a sensitivity where effects as minimal as one part in a thousand become detectable.

This study validates that simple recurrent neural networks (SRNNs), trained to generate the next term in a sparse, causal sequence, exhibit task-switching capabilities in a 'causal switching' framework. Notably, these SRNNs were trained using only 10% of the available data and without explicit initialization. Furthermore, increasing the size of the neural network improved its performance significantly. We also investigated the impact of non-causal architectures on causal learning, revealing that such models struggled with capturing long-term dependencies. By analyzing the dynamics of successful causal learning in a simple 1D model, we demonstrated that certain neural configurations are essential for causal switching, a concept we then generalized to more complex problems.

This work delves into a particular class of nilpotent algebras that can be understood through a diagonal action with a generic stabilizer, also related to algebras with homogeneous nilpotent orbits. We establish connections between these geometric and categorical invariants and demonstrate how they interlock. Furthermore, we check these findings against examples within the realm of algebras representing singularities.

High-redshift Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs) exhibit extremely powerful and long-lasting relativistic jets. These jets are fed by the cosmic microwave background radiation at close ranges and the jets themselves at farther distances. To understand this development process, we've used 3D MHD simulations to model the interaction between the accretion flow and the jets, particularly focusing on radiation effects. Our results show that the thermal response to particle acceleration by an electric field does not significantly differ from non-radiative simulations up to 10 parsecs. However, the radiation cooling leads to narrower jets and larger areas of radiative feedback, particularly observable in high-energy and broadband observations of the interaction region.

In this commentary, I employ geometric and algebraic techniques to construct multiple lagrangians for classical gravity, highlighting their equivalence. Additionally, I highlight specific geometric characteristics associated with each constructed lagrangian.

Our new approach, PVDSP, addresses the challenge of registering picture volumes by leveraging both global and local features. PVDL utilizes symmetry-based features found in 2D images, and our novel framework combines this with matchable keypoint features from a volume to developing correspondence fields between image and pixel intensity patterns in 3D space. PVDL relies on two main components: integrating local features from 2D images into a 3D space and combining these with global features. Specifically, our approach uses bookkeeping strategies based on 3D SP-symmetry and sift keypoints to 3D features using estimated pose information. PVDL demonstrates superior performance over existing volume-based image intensity registration methods in experiments conducted on brain images.

Recent time-series photometry of the white dwarf binary SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, characterized by a 40.5-minute photometric cycle, revealed significant variations in light intensity due to the binary system's eclipses and the irregular star spot distribution. Using multi-color data, our analysis determined the system's properties, including the temperature, albedo, and radius of each component. Our results indicate that the binary consists of a approximately 2,300 K white dwarf with a about 9000 K secondary component. By incorporating light curve modeling, our calculations refined the system's geometric parameters and confirmed the inclination of 89.45 degrees. Additionally, our analysis estimated the distances to the system using both black body and greybody models, yielding values of 1,030 parsecs and 1,070 parsecs respectively, consistent with a previously published parallax measurement of 1,060 parsecs. Our work contributes to understanding the dynamics and evolution of double-degenerate binaries like SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, facilitating further research into such celestial systems.

Global aggregation methods, widely employed in machine learning and decision-making processes, utilize averaging methods such as summing, combining, or selecting dominant characteristics from multiple instances. These techniques rely on global aggregation functions that are both symmetric and monotonic. However, the limitations of traditional methods become apparent when dealing with complex or conflicting data, leading to subpar performance. This research introduces a comprehensive framework for assessing and comparing global aggregation functions through the lens of optimal transport theory. The proposed framework's strengths lie in its ability to facilitate symmetric and monotonic aggregation while allowing for a systematic evaluation of potential alternatives. By incorporating measures of uncertainty and risk, the framework expands the range of viable global aggregation options. Furthermore, the framework facilitates the discovery of aggregations tailored to specific conditions or preferences. Numerical experiments demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed method in identifying global aggregations adapted to uncertain data.

The characteristics of galaxies hosting different types of active galactic nuclei (AGN) are analyzed. Data from the SDSS galaxy survey are used to compare elliptical and spiral galaxy properties, including galaxy inclination and morphology, among various AGN types. Our findings reveal that in spherical galaxies, Type 1 AGN exhibit faster black hole mass growth compared to Type 2 AGn, whereas no significant differences were observed among radio-loud sources. Furthermore, we found that Type 1 AGN in disk galaxies tend to host inclined galaxies, whereas Type 2 AGN are more likely to be located in face-on galaxies. This suggests an alignment between the accretion disk and the host galaxy disk, which supports the scenario that the host galaxy disk absorbs and blocks the direct jets, thereby transforming a Type 1 AGN into a Type 2 AGN when a major galaxy merger occurs leading to an inclined or spherical galaxy.

This paper investigates special rotations within the 4-dimensional Euclidean space E^4, specifically those with flat tangent maps that satisfy the 1-type condition. We establish crucial and comprehensive criteria for identifying these rotation groups. Additionally, we identify and categorize all rotation groups that satisfy the 1-type condition and possess flat tangent maps.

This study investigates whether self-supervised depth estimation is an effective alternative to pre-training a convolutional neural network through image classification. The researchers find that using depth estimation as a pre-training method encourages the network to learn more robust features, particularly in areas unrelated to depth, such as monochromatic images. The decision is grounded in an analysis of the inherent properties of the tasks involved, which reveals significant overlap between the tasks of depth estimation and semantic segmentation. Moreover, the study's results demonstrate that the various components of a monocular depth estimation model play distinct roles and contribute synergistically to its overall performance. The study's code is now available on the PyTDepth GitHub repository.

Time-series data plays a crucial role in monitoring changing processes and events, enabling timely decision-making. However, visual analysis alone is often insufficient to detect patterns and make trends understandable, particularly in the context of rising data availability. To address this challenge, we propose TCube, a novel system that generates human-readable time-series stories using large language models, enabling the identification of anomalies and trends even in domain-specific data sets. TCube employs a unique approach that creates synthetic time-series data accompanied by invented stories, training LLMs to detect anomalies and maintain fairness across different domains. Our evaluations reveal TCube's effectiveness in uncovering temporal anomalies and domains with unusual characteristics, outperforming existing methods and showcasing its potential to highlight domains requiring further investigation, as seen in our analysis of COVID-related datasets.

Our report presents the latest findings from the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider on the study of rare phenomena associated with bottom mesons, including a specific analysis of charm symmetry in those mesons. Our assessments encompass studies concerning the violation of both CP symmetry and unique decay patterns within particles that are the antiparticle of their own, as well as in the rare occurrence of a certain type of decay. To aid in comparing results, we have also included comprehensive tables and have clarified the distinctions between the ATLAS experiment's findings and those of other experimental groups, as well as the theoretical predictions from the standard model.
On a Cayley tree of arbitrary degree and branching degree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel types of Gibbs measures that exhibit both periodic and mildly periodic characteristics.

A specific type of hyperbolic problem, known as Cauchy issues, has been studied, particularly those with coefficients that vary significantly. A new class of spaces with log-Lipschitz characteristics was introduced, allowing for the definition of solutions to the equation $\partial_{tt}u=a(t)\Delta u=f,$ even when they decay globally. Under certain conditions, it's demonstrated that the coefficients $a(t)$, which are bounded and have specific spatial smoothness, generate a global solution unique in the space of decaying globally functions. These results are relevant to global problems with log-Lipschitz coefficients. A crucial aspect involves defining solutions as distributions, which, however, often lead to singularities due to small characteristics. The proposed framework addresses this challenge, particularly for the given equation, and confirms global well-posedness, which is relevant to small log-Lipschitz coefficients. This work confirms a particular case of a conjecture proposed by Igvol'chak and displays the limited impact of nonlinearity in the given equation, which was also highlighted by demonstrating results with linear coefficients.

WSD, or Word Division, serves as a fundamental task in NLP with pivotal importance. The accuracy of WSD heavily depends on precise character-level input encoding. The existing most advanced WSD models utilize character-based encoding. However, this approach has its drawbacks as it fails to take advantage of the inherent word-based nature of the language. In contrast, we propose extended Short-Term Memory encoding, which leverages previous reading progress and character importance to improve WSD performance, especially in the case of Japanese. By incorporating this novel encoding method, we have observed a substantial boost in WSD accuracy for multiple Japanese languages, including standard Japanese and texts incorporating Chinese characters. Moreover, this extended short-term memory encoding can be widely applied to various language processing tasks that are sensitive to input encoding.

Stack Overflow's vast repository of questions continues to attract unresolved inquiries, particularly those beyond the expertise of its community of developers and future professionals. Due to privacy restrictions, existing research on development community knowledge and expertise has been constrained by available dataset limitations. In this study, we analyze public knowledge accessed through Stack Overflow answers, examining the external links shared in responses to understand how community expertise is communicated. By combining a large-scale Stack Overflow dataset with web crawl metadata, we reveal the sources of these external links, exposing a significant gap between creators and consumers of content, as link creators lack awareness of content consumption patterns. Furthermore, we identify underlying patterns and dependencies among these external links and their source domains, and evaluate the popularity and impact of shared content using metrics such as frequency, popularity, and impact.

There have been multiple attempts to model the galaxy's age and composition, but recent data from the Milky Way's halo show a significant discrepancy.  The attempts to resolve this inconsistency have been largely unsatisfactory due to several issues.  The halo's composition can't be accurately predicted by simple models because they can't account for the effects of intergalactic exchanges.  The "self-enrichment" hypothesis is flawed due to the lack of adequate mechanisms to supply the necessary matter.  The proposed solutions involving the migration of matter from the galaxy's outer areas and an extra source of light are both unsupported by additional data and do not resolve the underlying problem of age and composition inconsistencies.

This paper explores the establishment of a comprehensive climate data repository that facilitates informed discussions on climate change by aggregating relevant data. To bridge the gap between researchers and policymakers, who often face difficulties accessing dispersed climate data, there is a need for a unified platform to share clinical knowledge. By promoting collaborative research and data-sharing among clinicians, the Climate Data Repository will empower scientists to conduct thorough analyses and reveal underlying climate patterns. Ultimately, actionable insights derived from these studies can support evidence-based decision-making in climate policy formulation.

Domain adaptation issues frequently arise in medical natural language processing tasks, particularly those involving clinical notes. These problems can be mitigated by focusing on key information and disregarding domain-specific jargon. Building upon this concept, our research introduces SymEventSet, a symbolic neural network designed for the general extraction of symptom events across diverse medical domains. By filtering out redundant and uninformative characters, SymEventSet enhances domain-independent representation learning. Through experimentation across four distinct datasets from different clinical settings, SymEventSet consistently outperformed established baseline methods without requiring any domain-specific training. Notably, it achieved a remarkable 71.4% F1-score on SymSet, a symptom extraction task based on clinical encounter texts, surpassing strong baseline models by 16.1 percentage points.

Our proposed Deep Reinforcement Learning model utilizes state information from a self-driving vehicle's onboard LiDAR and camera systems to determine the optimal speed and direction of movement. This design aims to prevent collisions with obstacles while minimizing journey time. Since re-calibrating sensor systems in real-world conditions can be costly, our model leverages RiRi, a simulation environment that mimics real vehicle perceptions and extracts feature information from raw data. We tested our model against existing approaches in various real-world scenarios and achieved better results in terms of avoiding obstacles and reducing travel time.

The growing number of IoT devices with limited resources necessitates efficient machine learning algorithms that operate within tight power constraints. By harnessing the capabilities of spiking neural networks, which can mimic biological neurons' behavior, significant efficiency gains are possible in image classification tasks. In this study, we adapt the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire neuron model to utilize Random Neural Networks for tackle the challenging problem of efficient and accurate classification. Our work expands on previous research by incorporating hysteresis and negative rates into the RNN's leaky integrate-and-fire model. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed classifier achieves a remarkable balance between accuracy and computational efficiency, outperforming existing methods while requiring minimal power to operate.

The thermal properties of Strange Quark Stars with internal magnetic fields are investigated, assuming elevated temperatures and perfect alignment of the star's mass with its strong magnetic field. In the presence of finite temperature effects, traditional Star Models exhibiting phase transitions are rendered obsolete. Instead, we employ two advanced models, namely the Hellings-Nicolaidou and the Holopainen-Vuorinen models, to determine the impact of temperature and magnetic field on Strange Quark Stars. Our results indicate that these factors cause the star's mass and radius to contract, while its surface energy density and chemical potential demonstrate an inverse relationship with temperature and magnetic field intensity.

Pando is a Caltech-developed volunteer computing framework that harnesses the power of browser-based agents to solve NP-hard problems. It functions similarly to distributed frameworks like BOINC and Slingshot, but distinguishes itself by enabling individual voluntary computing efforts rather than relying on machines to submit multiple instances. By utilizing a straightforward submission process and browser interfaces, Pando makes it accessible for a broad range of users to participate in scientific research, including students and those on single-machine setups. By focusing on the human element, Pando aims to pave the way for enhanced agent-human collaborative solving of complex problems. By collecting and sharing insights from voluntary computing sessions, Pando also provides valuable data on volunteer computing demographics, efficacy, and user behavior.

Relying on the superior performance of nonlinear eigenproblems solvers based on rational interpolation methods like Riemann-Riesz and Krylov acceleration, the concept of adaptivity is introduced. This approach involves strategically increasing the size of the interpolation data whenever improvement in the approximate solutions is anticipated. An efficient implementation of this strategy is established within the MINRES solver framework, allowing for improved performance and adaptivity. As a result, a more compact interpolation data set is achieved, particularly in scenarios involving nonlinear eigenproblems situated close to real eigenvalues, yielding better performance comparable to infinite interpolation data sets while maintaining accurate solutions and approximate acceleration of the solution convergence rates.

This study explores the complexity of all $\beta$-shifts, an important class of irreducible irreducible irreducible irreducible irreducible irreducible irreducible irreducible irreducible shift dynamical systems, and demonstrates that they either exhibit maximal or intermediate complexity. The paper characterizes the intermediate $\beta$shifts, initially identified as a distinct category separate from avaricious $\beta$shifts, and reveals the properties of avaricious shifts with gaps in their greedy expansions, which includes all intermediate shifts. The dynamics of these shifts are investigated in detail.

To enhance the transparency of complex machine learning models like Random Forests and AdaBoost, we developed a novel method to create disentangled attribution graphs that clearly display variable interactions. This method was applied to classify bank loans and detect anomalies in the Minimalistic Automotive Fault Code dataset. Our approach offers a more clear and understandable visualization of the trained models compared to contemporary attribution methods, while also verifying its consistency and stability.

Machine learning models can benefit from federated learning, a technique that allows a server to train across multiple data sources without requiring that data to be centralized. Building upon this concept, we propose an innovative federated learning framework that leverages user hardware and software security features, specifically trusted execution environments, to support training across decentralized data sources. By integrating support for plaintext data within Trusted Platform Modules and leveraging remote attestation, our hardware and software components can facilitate encrypted communication between clients and the server without the limitations imposed by encryption. We believe this new framework will be beneficial for clients who have access to secure hardware and want to conduct privacy-preserving ML training. To validate our system, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation using various deep learning models and noticed minimal accuracy and computational overhead compared to traditional training methods.

Modern processors utilize highly complex optimization techniques that require users to select a range of complex operators. Evaluating the impact of these operators involves examining the resulting machine code and system performance, which can be time-consuming and labor-intensive for complex processors and applications. This paper introduces an automated framework that streamlines this process by integrating existing tools and streamlining the workflow into a single, automated pipeline. The proposed framework's effectiveness is demonstrated with real-world applications on the AMD Zen 3 processor, revealing that most operations have negligible impact, while others yield noticeable improvements, such as reducing memory access latency through data placement optimizations and enhancing vectorization and branch prediction through data dependency reordering.

One key issue preventing the widespread adoption of microservices is the unpredictability of their execution times. This problem can be exacerbated by the shared nature of cloud infrastructure, leading to varying levels of resource availability and unpredictable behavior. While traditional Quality-of-Service systems attempt to mitigate this issue by reserving specific resources for individual applications, this approach can result in inefficient use of available infrastructure and increased costs. A more adaptable solution is needed to handle the complexities of loosely coupled, highly dynamic applications while maintaining temporal quality of service. 

To overcome these challenges, we introduce Timeloops, a cutting-edge executive module that enables temporal quality of service in containerized environments. Timeloapses automatically discovers call policies to minimize the completion time of program runs, thereby improving end-to-end temporal quality of service without manual configuration or knowledge of the underlying application logic. This self-adjusting module adapts to changes in the underlying infrastructure, resulting in enhanced resource utilization, lower service costs, and increased application throughput. In a real-world test of Timeloaps on a popular web application, we observed improved response times and a 20% increase in application throughput. Additionally, Timeloaps has demonstrated its ability to translate learned call policies into actionable policies, further enhancing its practical value.

This research explores the outcomes of linear classifiers operating within commodity space forms defined by positive linear dependence among commodities. To achieve broader applicability, Bounded Rationality Theory and Axiomatic Welfare Economics are extended to accommodate this context. We examine the effects of group consistency and separation requirements on commodity space properties, which resemble properties of curved spaces due to their homogeneity. Our analysis also considers the implications of commodity diversification on classifier behavior, which reveals non-linear behavior despite the use of linear classification methods. We establish that classes must be separated by a hyperplane projectable onto a simplex to akinumerical behavior, whereas a diversification axis influences behavior projectable onto a ball with curved boundary in the commodity space.

Our previous work demonstrated that a substantial number of long-lived stellar configurations can persist in the gravitational sphere influence of a massive black hole. The underlying concept involves arranging stars such that they reside within the black hole's inner region, while their orbital periods are greatly shortened due to their increased proximity. The arrangement's outer boundary is dictated by the point of intersection between the spheres of gravitational control for the black hole and each star. However, these intersections form an elongated, flattened shape, rather than being perfectly spherical. As a result, numerous short-lived configurations arise from the uneven distribution of stars inside this boundary. To address this issue, we have now refined our approach to account for these complexities. Through our revised analysis, we have found that the density of stars inside the boundary is significantly lower than in the original study. The findings indicate a much larger population of long-lived stellar configurations than initially thought. The refined calculations have been encoded into the GALAXYLAB software for use in a broader range of applications.

This paper presents a simple model predictive control strategy that leverages prior knowledge of a system's dynamics to make informed decisions for future actions. It argues for the benefit of anticipating and preparing for future scenarios rather than solely reacting to present conditions. We illustrate the approach using a basic simulation, such as managing resources or making decisions related to gender, housing, or other categorizations.

Unmixing high-dimensional data often relies on independent component analysis, a method based on the assumption that data results from a linear combination of independent sources. Most real-world data cannot be accurately represented using standard Gaussian distributions, leading researchers to propose a non-compressible approach that better captures complex data patterns. The comment presents a compressible approach by considering data based on $\ell_q$-norm ($0<q<1$) and establishing a lattice structure to find optimal sources, ultimately proving its computational feasibility through dynamic programming and demonstrating the effectiveness of this compressible model over its non-compressible counterpart.

We examine a scenario where two species compete over diverse habitats, each with distinct dynamics - some chaotic and others orderly. The competition is further complicated by a trade-off between fighting within the same habitat type (intertype competition) and invading other types (intraspecific). By simplifying the system into two components, we develop an analytical method to determine outcomes of the competition and the conditions under which species coexist through repeated colonization of different chaotic and orderly landscapes.

We show that a specific construction combining regional von Neumann algebras associated with overlapping regions yields a tensor category, which is isomorphic to the abelian quantum double model's topological category. This finding allows us to determine the natural symmetry of this tensor category.

Exploring the interplay between magnons, photons, and phonons in cavity magnomechanics presents an excellent opportunity to create and investigate complex quantum correlations in quantum information applications. However, dissipation caused by the system and its environment often hampers magnon-photon-phonon entanglement. Our research demonstrates that coherent feedback circuits can enhance the generation and maintenance of such entanglement. Specifically, connecting the magnon and phonon components to external microwave resonators, which form a logical NOT gate, allows active coupling and realgar compensation of dissipation effects. To optimize these connections and amplify the tripartite entanglement formed by magnons, photons, and phonons, we employed the DMRG method. Our findings reveal that coherent feedback not only enhances the duration and degree of steady-state and dynamic entanglement but also compensates for the magnitude of dissipation influencing the system, thereby improving quantum resource generation for potential applications.

This study presents one-loop calculations for all triple-collinear splittings in the QCD framework, within the double precision scheme. Calculations were conducted in a formally corrected dimension regime and scheme, with contributions from all flavor types and colors. The derived operators facilitate compilation of numerically evaluated splitting functions and higher-order correction terms and are compatible with existing higher-order terms already established in the literature. Additionally, this compilation incorporates lower-order splitting functions and their associated corrections up to third order.

We have positive characteristic cases of Neron Desingularization positive generalizations in one-dimensional local rings, which are a new outcome stemming from Zhang's work, and we employ this finding to prove the Neron Desingularization Neron Skolem Lemma's translation version in one-dimensional local rings, which was proven via a diverse method previously.

The Indonesian archipelago's sundials were recently preserved by implementing a time recording system, leveraging the solar positions and their impact on day-to-day time variations. By analyzing the chronological changes in sundial time from 2000 to 2023, the project demonstrated the significance of historical sundials in understanding the Earth's changing solar position due to its orbital dynamics. This approach effectively showcases the natural time variations resulting from the planet's orbital characteristics.

This study presents a novel coexistence of D2D communication that leverages an Intellect Reflecting Surface to simultaneously manage data transfer and energy distribution within a single D2D network. By integrating RIS into D2D comnet, we explore its potential to address the inherent energy limitations of D2D devices. Our proposed framework incorporates both active and passive RIS elements, and employs a joint optimization strategy to simultaneously enhance the data transmission rate and device energy efficiency through coordinated RCS configuration and power distribution. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated by comparing it with alternative methods that either omit RIS or utilize only active RIS, highlighting the superiority of IIESC with both types of RIS in a various scenarios.

Three-dimensional flow fields can be mapped in just a few seconds by synchronizing multiple Planar Laser Doppler Velocimetry (PLDV) planes, but gathering this data takes significantly longer when done sequentially using a single PLDV source. Our proposed single-point control system allows for the efficient collection of two-dimensional flow velocities by rapidly switching between different PLDV planes under unified control. By rapidly switching the illumination region's position and timing velocity measurements taken from each plane, we can achieve high temporal resolution for each velocity profile. This single-point control approach was successfully tested on a developing boundary layer in a wind tunnel, demonstrating its capability to capture accurate three-dimensional flow velocity profiles.

This memo explores the computational complexity of evaluating the spectra of certain classes of matrices, specifically those involving combinations of unary, binary, and alternating relations. We introduce two new types of alternating relations: one where the second element equals the first ($id_1$) and another where it equals its complement ($id_2$). By examining all possible combinations of these relations, we classify and analyze the complexity of calculating the spectra for corresponding matrix classes and provide canonical forms for each set to simplify computations.

A new hardware device called the waveplate programmable phase disc (WPPD) has been introduced to modify the phase of electron waves in a transmission electron microscope. Researchers discovered that inserting the WPPD into a transmission electron microscope allows for correcting chromatic aberrations in the device's image transfer function in a computationally efficient manner. They found that even limited sets of waveplates in the WPPD can significantly improve the impact of chromatic aberrations and minimize the negative effects in the transmission electron microscope's image transfer function. Ultimately, WPPD technology enables improved high-resolution transmission electron microscopy performance.

A fundamental challenge in quantum physics is calculating properties of atomic and molecular systems using quantum mechanics. This work achieves two main objectives: Firstly, it derives a general formula for the energy of $N$ non-relativistic particles confined within an arbitrary potential. This formula can be easily implemented on computers using the plane wave basis set approach. Secondly, the study introduces a novel convergence acceleration formula tailored for solving time-independent Schrodinger's equation through the plane wave basis set method. This innovative formula appears to enhance existing convergence acceleration techniques in quantum mechanics.

This paper explores the properties of random walks within a $d$-dimensional lattice, specifically the behaviors of N steps in a random walk starting from the origin of $\mathbb{Z}^d$. We focus on the count of unique positions attainable in this random walk after N steps, denoted as $W_N(d)$, and we examine the ratios of these counts across different dimensions and step numbers. In addition, this paper introduces recursive formulas for calculating $W_N(d)$ and validates these formulas using properties related to stochastic walk behaviors. We verify our results using a computer algebra system to ensure their accuracy.

This research inquires into the detailed geometry and quasinormal mode spectrum of a polymer black hole within the framework of loop quantum gravity. We investigate how the transition function impacts the hole's structure in its far-distant and event horizon regions through expansion and expansion rate analysis. To understand the hole's properties, we also examine the spacetime and gravitational radius perturbations. Furthermore, our study focuses on how the mass and transition function influence the quasinormal mode spectrum, and we explore how this spectrum can aid in distinguishing between different polymer models and distinguishing quantum black holes from traditional general relativity black holes through observational data from gravitational waves.

The shielding of electric fields in doped graphene is analyzed numerically, 
resulting in a dielectric function that can be used to calculate various thermal 
properties. This includes the use of molecular dynamics simulations, a classical 
approach valid at sufficiently high temperatures, to calculate specific heat 
within the random phase approximation. The computed thermal properties agree 
well with experimental data, allowing for a continuous explanation of 
graphene's thermal behavior across a wide range of temperatures, from insulating 
to metal-like states.

We present a method to generate natural, context-dependent speech using a masking technique that leverages contextual information from spoken dialogue. Our approach builds upon masking regions within the sequence to incorporate contextual information, specifically employing a diagonal masking method and neural structure similar to that of the Transformer. We compare our method to a traditional attention-based model and show through extensive experiments that utilizing contextual information improves the quality of synthesized speech. Additionally, our research indicates that preserving the original order of the sequence using the diagonal masking method yields the most optimal results.

Despite the success of supervised learning in controlled environments, their ability to adapt to unforeseen situations is severely limited. While current methods can to an extent deal with slight changes in input, they struggle significantly when faced with completely new scenarios. It's well-established that pre-training models on extensive datasets and utilizing large latent spaces can enhance performance on diverse applications and facilitate adaptation to new situations. Building upon these concepts and hidden Markov models (HMMs), we developed the space projection predictive reasoning (SPPR) framework, which learns a space of object configurations that maximizes the likelihood of predicting a system's future state from its current state. By employing an unsupervised, self-supervised approach, SPPR can uncover the underlying structure of data without needing labeled examples. We tested SPPR on creating a basic representation of 2D scenes and successfully applied it to design a controller for navigating a robot through unfamiliar environments. Furthermore, we demonstrated its capability to generate a latent representation of scenes in the AlphaGo fashion, along with its predictive power.

Machine learning models rely heavily on vast amounts of training data, which is often sourced from online platforms. The security of this data is compromised when it is hosted on malicious generative frameworks, making models susceptible to person-in-the-middle attacks during training. These attacks manipulate learning algorithms by intercepting data, leading to severe breaches of machine learning classifier reliability. The consequences are exacerbated in real-world applications, such as facial expression recognition, where poisoned training data can cause life-threatening errors. This study investigates how these assaults impact the performance of machine learning classifiers and explores potential safeguards. The findings reveal that models trained through interactions with malicious frameworks suffer significant performance degradation, which significantly outpaces traditional poisoning attacks. The research demonstrates thatpoisoned models can be detected using analysis of their decision boundaries. Additionally, switching to secure data sources or limiting training epochs can mitigate the severity of the attacks. The study's insights into assault duration and decision boundaries provide valuable information for understanding the vulnerabilities of machine learning algorithms.

Climate change is the most pressing threat to global sustainability, yet its abstract effects make it difficult for the average person to grasp its urgency, allowing doubters to capitalize on this confusion. Climate denialism often takes the form of conspiracy theories that claim a secretive group is fabricating the crisis for political or financial gain. This genre of climate denialism has its roots in government-backed disinformation campaigns from the 1970s, but it has since evolved beyond its government-sponsored origins. This study examines the characteristics of conspiracy theories discussed on social media by analyzing over 13 million Twitter posts from 2016 to 2019 using a Python-based web scraping approach and Natural Language Processing, revealing a resurgence of perceived government-driven narratives despite their discontinued climate policies.

A study of shadow matter production in conjunction with a top quark is conducted using data from 13 TeV proton-proton collisions recorded by the CMS detector at CERN. The analyzed dataset corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 93.01 fb$^{-1}$, collected during 2016. Two investigation paths are considered, each involving a distinct top quark production method and distinct decay patterns for a hypothetical shadow matter particle. The analysis either observes $25.2$ pb for a shadow matter particle mass of $50$ GeV and coupling strength $0.1$ when this particle decays into a top quark and a photon, or observes $14.7$ pb for a shadow matter particle mass of $50$ GeV and coupling strength $0.1$ when this particle decays into a top quark and a Z boson, which further decays into a pair of photons. The analysis path featuring the intermediate Z boson decay into a photon pair exhibits superior sensitivity.

In an n-triangulated category with suspension functor Σ, we establish isomorphisms Σ^n ≅ Ψ and Ψ ≅ Σ, allowing us to define a triangulated category-trianglement. We then define a special type of n-triangulated category that satisfies specific duality properties through exact n-triangles, and we determine the conditions under which this category meets all required criteria for being a valid triangulated category.

The impact of choosing a field of study on fields' return on investment has been utilized as evidence for the role of instrumented variables in influencing fields' return on investment.  In order to strengthen the influence of instrumented variables, we developed a model that relies solely on fields' return on investment being influenced by fields' return on investment.  In this model, fields' return on investment are influenced by ability and preferences, but fields' return on investment are not influenced by ex-ante fields' return on investment.  In order to accommodate fields' return on investment, the ex-ante fields' return on investment must be influenced by an external factor that is independent of abilities and preferences, such as enrollment in a particular field of study.  This model provides an explanation for returns to fields of study and the choice of instrumented variables, such as universities offering fields of study.  In addition, this model has broader implications for fields' return on investment, such as education policy analysis and fields' return on investment.

Production of super $J/\psi$ particles utilizing nanometer-scale copper targets enables the creation of an intense $J/\psi$ beam, combined with a helical magnetic field, leading to a highly concentrated trap of slow particles such as antineutrons, antiprotons, and hyperons ($e^+e^-$ annihilation products excluded). This unique setup enables a wide range of nuclear and particle physics experiments with significant new potential advancements.

The speed at which material falls toward the central point of a binary system surrounded by a flat disk is approximately the speed at which the inner binary's orbit decays. By combining this inner speed with the speed at which the outer binary's orbit shrinks, we can calculate the overall accretion rate. Tests using numerical models have shown that this approach is reasonably accurate. The overall accretion rate is mostly determined by how quickly the outer and inner binaries shrink, specifically by comparing the ratios of their respective orbital periods. If the difference in these periods is less than a factor of ten, the rate is primarily affected by the outer model speed, otherwise it's mostly determined by the inner speed. This rate generally decreases by a factor of about 0.7 for each difference in periods, although there are occasional spikes of higher values at specific patterns of interaction between the three bodies. The overall trend is that as the outer and inner differences in these periods increase, the rate of decay of the outer and inner orbits decreases, specifically by following the relationship of (Δp)^(0.7).

The consideration of cosmological models relies heavily on the underlying framework in which they are formulated. While General Relativity provides the most well-established framework, alternative theories such as Lattice Gravity introduce different formulations that necessitate careful examination. This work delves into the characteristics of these models by examining their inherent features, specifically focusing on their flat nature. By analyzing the geometric properties in a lattice formulation, we investigate why certain outcomes are predetermined or 'hard-coded' rather than emerging as spontaneous results. This analysis is pertinent not only to cosmological models but also to understanding why the universe exhibits such flatness today. Additionally, we explore the relationship between Lattice Gravity and Lattice Field Theory when dealing with matter fields, which could inform the development of new, flat universe models based on non-dynamical constraints.

This paper proposes a novel two-stage method for partitioning images, where the initial phase employs a variational model based on a new edge-preserving image reconstruction method, followed by a refinement stage that enhances segmentation accuracy through a length-based functional optimization and corresponding numerical solutions. The integration of these models yields precise image partitioning results, which outperform those obtained through the traditional Snavely model.

Heavy spin-polarized particles, the ancient quasars in particular, can interact with certain very light particles known as ultralight bosons. This interaction may cause the particles to absorb rotational energy from the quasars. By analyzing data on this energy loss across a large dataset of 10,000 quasars, collected by two telescopes and occurring between 2015 and 2019, researchers have identified a specific range of boson properties. This energy loss data excludes certain masses of these ultralight bosons and their associated coupling strengths to a force carried by these particles. This is the first study of its type to utilize data on energy loss from spins of quasars to identify the properties of these bosons.

Creating artificial intelligence inspired by the human brain has become a crucial area of research in recent years. Utilulating spiking neural networks (SNNs) holds great potential in achieving this goal due to their ability to capture complex patterns in data and process them efficiently. A notable processor designed to efficiently handle large-scale SNNs is Intel's Loihi, which outperforms traditional multi-core processors by a factor of ten in terms of power consumption for brain-inspired tasks. To accurately simulate tasks on the Loihi processor, an effective and precise emulator is required. In this paper, we describe a newly developed emulator that accurately models the behavior of the Loihi processor by leveraging a high-speed simulator that models neural networks.

In 2019, an analysis of data from the Hi-C instrument identified a magnetic field disturbance known as an microflare, characterized by multiple sources emitting noise bursts. These bursts displayed significant temporal and spatial coherence across four distinct sources, suggesting a common evolutionary pattern. Frequency and duration of oscillations from the sources showed contrasting trends, with two increasing and two decreasing in step with rising source intensity. Furthermore, the bursts displayed synchronized onsets and durations, suggesting unified triggering mechanisms. This study suggests the magnetic field reconfiguration likely involved reconnection of nested field lines supported by stress accumulation from sheared motions.

Researchers have created a innovative and space-efficient magnetic optical trap with all its components on a two-dimensional plane. This specific magnetic optical trap features planar integrated components and utilizes a unique elliptical radial magnetic field, generated by specially designed coil structures. By combining this approach with specialized software and hardware, scientists can efficiently optimize its performance metrics. Consequently, they achieved remarkable results within 10 microseconds, trapping $^{87}\textrm{Rb}$ atoms at high populations with an individually measured ellipsity of 0.66. Additionally, the team developed a new method using Newton's method to simplify the calculation of confining magnetic field parameters. Furthermore, they successfully implemented a two-dimensional magnetic optical trap configuration, enabling precise control over trapped atoms in the optical direction through digitally controlled polarization switching.

The impact of finite-sized origin on steady accretion flows onto non-rotating and rotating black holes is investigated.  Origin radii as large as approximately 10 times the horizon area are considered without introducing artificial velocity or angular momentum restrictions.  Velocity and angular momentum profiles emerging from the origin significantly determine whether matter falls directly into the black hole, escapes to infinity, or becomes trapped in the near-horizon region as an unstable disk-like state.  In the case of non-rotating black holes, decreased origin size leads to increased accretion rates, with origin velocities having little effect.  Conversely, for rotating black holes, decreased origin size results in increased accretion rates up to a certain point, after which further decreases lead to reduced accretion rates.

Consider a two-level atom initially at rest near a thin mirror, capable of absorbing and re-emitting light from its ground to excited state transition. Upon receiving an excitation, the atom's movement within the vicinity of the mirror influences its subsequent emission patterns, deviating from standard stationary emission principles. Specifically, at short, resonant distances, the atom's motion can induce variable emission probabilities based on its direction and distance from the mirror, often resulting in enhanced emission rates that can exceed free-space standard rates. Notably, this effect is strongly direction-dependent, often reversed based on the atom's position relative to the mirror, and also depends on the atom's excitation velocity, exhibiting characteristics similar to Doppler excitation. However, this phenomenon primarily arises from modification of the atom's interaction with its surrounding environment during excitation, rather than a combination of stationary emission probabilities, thereby distinguishing it from traditional Doppler effects.

Recent observations from Maunakea and Cerro Paranal have uncovered 11 massive stars exceeding 40,000 suns, nestled among younger counterparts within the Westerlund 2 cluster's vicinity. Although these stars likely formed as part of Westerlund 2, their associated light curves and spectral characteristics suggest they might be giant stars with unique properties. To better understand these stars, we analyzed high-resolution spectra, which led to the calculation of their masses, temperatures, gravities, masses, luminosities, and evolutionary stages. Notably, our data indicates these giants are not consistent with the standard single-star evolutionary models starting from the main sequence. To the best of our knowledge, this discovery represents the first instance of single stars with masses above 40,000 suns in the advanced red super giant stage. To account for the discrepancies, we propose two potential explanations: either these stars shed a significant portion of their original mass during the common envelope phase early in their lives, or they have undergone late-stage mass transfer through binary interactions.

This study investigates the existence of ground state solutions in $H^2(\mathbb{R}^N)$ for a biharmonic Choquard equation, where the nonlinearity reaches an exponential critical threshold. Under the condition of $1 < N \le 4$, we establish that standard ground state solutions exist for this type of equation. Our findings extend existing work on this topic, particularly in relation to the Strichartz critical threshold.

Deep learning has significantly advanced handwritten document restoration, yet current approaches often yield subpar results characterized by residual artifacts and blurred edges. These issues can hinder subsequent tasks such as optical character recognition and limit human accessibility for handwritten documents. Existing methods primarily rely on a single recovery task, resulting in inconsistent handwriting style and failure to address multiple degradation tasks simultaneously. Furthermore, they do not effectively incorporate prior knowledge, such as character structure and spatial layout. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel approach that employs a multi-task adversarial network to tackle various restoration tasks while leveraging prior knowledge to improve overall performance. Our method involves constructing characteristic and spatial prior maps, which guide a generative adversarial network to restore original image features. Our experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over state-of-the-art techniques, with a approximately 10 dB increase in structural similarity metric for our primary restoration task.

The increasing reliance on digital systems is accompanied by a surge in electronically stored data. However, issues such as data privacy, ownership, and ownership rights remain unresolved. One effective means of addressing these concerns is through the adoption of Identity Card extraction and processing, allowing individuals to access specific information on their own ID cards. This study proposes an ID document extraction method for Indonesian passports, driver's licenses, and national ID cards, leveraging low-cost OCR technology and affordable NLP-based post-analysis. The proposed approach utilizes easy-to-use, high-performance IDP NLP models, simplified by the removal of complex and computationally intensive components. The models were tested and compared against state-of-the-art ID document extraction methods, demonstrating their effectiveness in achieving competitive results.

In vehicular communication environments, channel estimation is hindered due to low信噪比 (SNR) and the intermittent nature of IEEE 802.11p standard preamble fields. Long guard intervals can mitigate SNR loss, yet they introduce significant transmission delays. This research leverages the time-localized preamble field data, enhanced by low-complexity temporal smoothing and a least-squares channel estimation approach, to improve efficiency without sacrificing performance.

Astronomers utilize color information from images to analyze data and understand the properties of celestial objects. However, processing large amounts of data in visible and infrared wavelengths can be time-consuming, particularly when using images taken by the Spitzer Space Telescope which are monochromatic. We've developed a neural network-based approach that leverages a single black-and-white image to quickly generate accurate color information by training it with data from the Hubble Space Telescope. This method takes into consideration the significant difference in resolution between the two telescopes by utilizing a super-resolution technique that generates realistic colors and improves image clarity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by comparing it to state-of-the-art models and showing its potential to efficiently produce colors for data cubes in just a fraction of the time, facilitating data visualization and analysis.

Optimizing complex neural networks often involves limitations due to their high number of parameters, which makes gradient-based optimization methods inefficient and prone to getting stuck in local minima. To overcome these challenges, we developed a novel universal estimation method that can accurately estimate any continuous function without requiring the complexity of gradient-based optimization. Our approach utilizes function value data to create simple polynomial models that quickly converge to the target function, eliminating the need to optimize their parameters. Through extensive experiments on universal estimators for both regression and classification problems, we demonstrated its superiority over traditional optimization methods, along with significant reductions in training time. The efficiency improvements stem from our approach's ability to simplify and generalize functions, which in turn minimizes its complexity. As applications of the optim estimator simplify functions, its performance continuously improves, enabling surprisingly accurate results even in basic linear functions.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECRCRC) plays a vital role in linking career development opportunities with other committees within the ECFA. Established in 2009 and comprising researchers in the early stages of their careers from various particle physics subfields, the ECRCRC organizes events and conducts surveys to gather insights on the professions of postdoc researchers and early career physicists. Through surveys and discussions, the committee maintains an ongoing dialogue with ECFA and other postdoc researchers about their career paths, ultimately contributing to career development schemes, especially for postdoc positions in Europe. As the ECRCRC's chairman, I will detail the committee's composition, structure, activities, and future plans for the 2021-2022 period.

Confining light into sub-wavelength spaces holds great potential for developing integrated optical devices and exploring new quantum phenomena. Historically, this has been achieved through plasmonic structures, but due to significant optical losses, their applications are limited. Recently, researchers have shown that this limitation can be overcome by using specially designed loss-cancelling dual-layer structures. Our research extends this concept by creating layered optical and plasmonic substrates to confine line waves at a boundary between two combined samples.
