Building upon the work of C\u{c}etinkaya et al. and C\u{c}etinkaya--Gualtieri, we examine geometric geometric T-duality within the framework of twisted tori, using hybrid approaches that combine $\mathbb{R}^d$ with twisted differential geometry tools. Our results show that endowing twisted differential structures with simple isomorphisms results in equivalent structures, reducing our findings to those of the category of twisted geometric type $(S,\Sigma)$ pairings. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula in supergeometry for the T-duality map associated with isomorphic twisted differential structures.

In Reinforcement Learning, CoObservation Learning allows agents to learn tasks more efficiently by observing each other's success, even if they don't see the process themselves. This is possible because they can gather valuable information from second-hand experiences, effectively using off-policy data. This paper's focus is on exploring how agents can learn CoObservation Learning by watching peers' success, without having to witness expert demonstrations. This is particularly useful in environments where obtaining expert demonstrations is challenging or costly. Additionally, the research delves into the fundamental challenges that arise when agents try to understand and leverage off-policy data to solve tasks, revealing the complexities involved in understanding and applying such data in practical scenarios.

This paper examines properties of Prediction-Avoidance Codes (PAC Codes), a type of prefix-free code widely utilized in data compression. PAC Codes are uniquely identified by their avoidance number, a integer h >= 1. What sets them apart is that none of their prefixes can be subdivided into at most h different parts. We introduce a new metric to compare these codes and investigate whether the previously established universal calculation method from [2] applies to them. As a natural extension of this study, we also investigate the performance of PAC Codes at large sizes.

Understanding how humans interact with objects within their environment is crucial for developing advanced AI systems capable of learning from unstructured and diverse visual data. Despite significant progress in tracking visible interactions between humans and objects in the field of computer vision, significant difficulties persist when dealing with complex scenes featuring obscured views of hands and objects. These challenges are particularly pronounced in uncontrolled environments such as the wilderness, where varying lighting, occlusions, and background noise pose significant obstacles. Recent research has shown that combining RGB cameras with depth sensors can effectively capture and analyze volumetric interactions, enabling more accurate tracking of hand-object interactions. Building on these findings, we introduce tracking and reconstruction techniques for hand-object interactions using point cloud sequences, which incorporate both temporal consistency and robustness to noise. These algorithms are paired with volumetric rendering to facilitate the visualization of interaction sequences, which can be used to train interaction regressors that predict how humans interact with objects based on hand and object poses. When evaluated on a novel dataset of wilderness scenes, our approach significantly surpasses existing methods in predicting valid interaction sequences, demonstrating remarkable robustness to noise and background noise with a prediction accuracy of 60%.

This study classifies all tail-triangle C-groups from Bourdon's list that feature exactly two interlacing axes. We discover five groups fitting these criteria, with four being crystallographic, and one noncrystallographic, possessing grade 4 complexity. Notably, the latter group can be represented by generators consisting of two 5-order rotation axes at an angle of $\frac{2\pi}{5}$, along with two 3-order rotation axes.

Designing robust robot depth cameras can be complicated by the need for precise depth calibration, end-effector position calculation, and view transformations, which often demands substantial data collection and labeling efforts. To mitigate these challenges, we present an unmarked system that automatically calibrates robots with depth cameras and accurately determines end-effector positions without the need for collected data. By leveraging a neural network, our approach learns the intrinsic and extrinsic parameters of the depth camera, end-effector position, and view transformation by combining depth images, 3D point clouds, and feedback from a robot's end-effector feedback mechanism. By optimizing these variables in unison, we simplify the process of setting up robots with depth cameras, streamlining calibration into a more efficient, dataless procedure. Additionally, our approach's ability to learn 3D scene representations and robot-specific end-effector positions simultaneously grants the system the adaptability to generalize across varying environments and objects, concluding that it can be applied to various robot systems across diverse tasks.

Under the assumption that treatment interference occurs within a defined radius of $K$ nearest neighbors, interference factors can be analyzed by comparing the differences between treated and control units within that interference radius. To validate these differences as indicative interference, significant differences must exist between the treated group and $K$ control neighbors, which in turn requires the ability to select an optimal $K$ value. A proposed estimator enables consistent estimation of the interference effect for any $K$ value, even when $K$ changes, allowing for the identification of optimal $K$ through model selection or confidence interval methods that account interference when $K$ is estimated.

Previous studies have shown that certain types of Dark Matter interactions can produce excessive neutrino emissions from neutron stars. However, this finding was later challenged due to an overlooked factor: the distinct behavior of these annihilations when occurring within the dense interior of a neutron star versus in lab experiments. This difference leads to increased emission rates compared to laboratory experiments. Researchers have recently identified two additional processes contributing to neutrino emissions, significantly altering their historical production through Dark Matter interactions.

The continuous improvement of image quality, complemented by the vast availability of deep-field galaxy catalog data, significantly accelerates our comprehension of the universe's expansion due to the effects of weak lensing. Nevertheless, accurately measuring the shapes of distant galaxies remains a significant technical challenge that demands sophisticated, user-friendly software. In response, we introduce ShapePipe, a cutting-edge software tool designed to streamline the process of shape measurement for research teams. In this study, we demonstrate the capabilities of ShapePipe by analyzing the shapes of galaxies within the UNIONS/CFIS dataset, encompassing nearly 1.7 million objects spanning redshifts from 0.1 to 1.5. Our investigation incorporates both a likelihood-based estimator, TweakReg, and template-matching algorithms, such as MFuZZ and MIROS, to ensure reliable shape assessments. Furthermore, we conduct an extensive validation of our workflow using both artificial and natural image datasets to account for systematic errors and evaluate the reliability of our method at varying redshift intervals. In particular, we identify and rectify potential biases in the shapes of galaxies, enabling precise and accurate shape corrections that are crucial for weak-lensing-based cosmological research.

Our findings build upon novel generalizations of Kronecker-Weyl theorems and extend previous work by Feng and Tseng concerning the mod 1 equidistribution of sequences. We extend these results to a broader class of functions, encompassing not only polynomial moduli but also higher-order-segment functions and logarithmic functions, and demonstrate the associated equidistribution outcomes and diophantine approximation outcomes.

We establish the rationality of certain local complete intersections defined by $k$-rational and $k$-Du Bois singularities. Furthermore, there's an exploration into the relationship between these intersections and specific varieties known as $k$-rational and $k$-Du Bois complete intersections.

It has long been believed that all magnets would exhibit either Ising, Heisenberg, or planar physics based on the arrangement of their spins. However, a new discovery reveals that a spin-1/2 Heisenberg model can exhibit Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations based on dimensionality and dimensionality-dependent exchange interactions in an applied field. This was observed in the compound BaCu$_2$(PO$_4$)$_2$ which exhibits strong anisotropy due to the arrangement of its magnetic ions. In the zero-field state, this material exhibits planar physics with strong correlations and is believed to exhibit critical behavior similar to the X-Y model in one dimension. In specific magnetic field configurations, however, this material exhibits Heisenberg physics with a exchange interaction in that direction that is stronger than the other two components, leading to strong spin fluctuations in that direction and similarities to the X-Y model in one dimension upon the application of a field parallel to that axis and the exhibit of BKT behavior both in magnetic susceptibility and specific heat measurements. This new phenomenon provides a theoretical basis on how 2D Heisenberg models can exhibit BKT physics without the need for geometric frustration.

We examine the feasibility of replacing dark matter with a combination of axions and sterile neutrinos, specifically with zero mass for the axions. To account for dark matter, this model necessitates a relatively large coupling of sterile neutrinos to photons, resulting in significant, observable effects. Consequently, it's forecasted that the space-based axion telescope TRACE-A will detect axions within this framework within a year of operation. Alternatively, the approach may offer valuable insights into axion and sterile neutrino properties, given established axion bounds.

Recent research has provided compelling evidence that certain quantum states are intrinsically complex, yet the exact measure of this complexity remains uncertain. The evidence so far relies on increasing the maximum number of simple components required to represent these states when they are combined, but these findings are limited to low-dimensional state sets. The researchers here establish a more robust proof by demonstrating that certain fundamental sets of complex magic states inherently possess a higher minimum number of components, applicable universally, and this value is significantly higher at a specific threshold of 1 + epsilon for any positive epsilon, and 3 for the specific case. The proof's validity is further substantiated by the availability of corresponding algorithms that efficiently approximate components of these states in polynomial time, with the number of components being directly proportional to the epsilon value raised to a power of 6, and applied here specifically to the well-known magic T-state.

This research explores a holographic dark energy model influenced by environmental factors, based on the Tsallis entropy principle, within a spatially non-uniform Quintessence framework represented as $\phi(x) = \phi_1(x) + \phi_2(ix)$. The study investigates two distinct forms of the model, either real or imaginary, and considers two types of spatial energy contributions: riemannian or fractional. The model's evolution is investigated using state equation parameters in a non-parametric form. The results indicate that a non-imagine Quintessence term paired with a fractional energy contribution leads to a more suitable model for describing the universe's evolution. Furthermore, this research pairs the model with a dynamic potential, and we observe that it is consistent with current observational data when the Tsallis parameter is 1.05 or less in riemannian models, and 0.95 in fractional models, assuming a power-law potential.

Large-scale surveys requiring substantial data processing are facing considerable challenges. As an essential component of the 1589-project LAMOST, we've analyzed four $K$2 plates from 2018, yielding over 10 million spectra for approximately 3.7 trillion possible combinations. Leveraging an advanced pipeline, we've extracted crucial data from these spectra, resulting in over 3 million entries with corresponding spectra, key findings from which reveal several interesting scientific outcomes. Firstly, our analysis has identified 27 Type II supernovae through distinct light curves and spectral characteristics, providing insights into their distribution and properties. Secondly, our data has facilitated the discovery of 900 variable stars exhibiting unique features, including some newly discovered objects. Moreover, our analysis has led to the identification of 900 novel candidates for exoplanet transients, while also finding around 90 objects likely associated with exoplanets and requiring further investigation. Moreover, our data has found around 900 objects likely associated with exoplanets, including some requiring further investigation. Lastly, our analysis has found around 90 objects likely associated with exoplanets, including some associated with known stars and exhibiting unexpected variability.

This research introduces a novel method for creating authentic random numbers by leveraging supply voltage underscaling in SRAMs, termed Supply Voltage Underscaling Supply Random Number generation (Supply Voltage -> Supply Random Number generation or TuVRNG for short). It exploits SRAM read instabilities by reducing the supply voltage below its nominal rating to induce read failures in SRAM memory cells. These induced failures serve as entropy sources for random number generation. To validate the technique's effectiveness, a technique was developed leveraging SRAM memory cells' probabilistic behavior. It utilizes the probability distribution of incorrect read values in SRAM memory cells. This approach extracts random bits via Successive Cancellation, employing a Markov Chain to demonstrate its convergence towards the uniform distribution. A theoretical and empirical analysis confirmed the proposed approach produces high-quality random numbers meeting industry standards, including NIST statistical tests. Furthermore, the design was empirically verified through actual hardware implementation and yielded promising performance in terms of entropy per access (approximately 3.5 bits) and latency (around 100ns).

A novel molecular single-electron resistive switch has been introduced, combining the stability of single-electron transistors with the compact molecular resistive switch. Through design examples utilizing alkene and ferrocene molecules, it's demonstrated that the stability of single-electron resistive switches relies on features that also provide thermal stability to single-electron transistors. One strategy to achieve this is employing redox moieties with minimal thermal stability but sufficient electrical stability to enable reliable single-electron transistor operation, which also results in robust single-electron resistive switch behavior. Results of finite-element simulations and the effects of model assumptions on resistive switch behavior are also presented.

The high-luminosity hadron colliders upcoming will require precise theoretical predictions to testSM physics in the heavy Higgs and weak boson scattering sectors beyond the standard model. Accurate calculations of certain scalar Feynman integrals are crucial for this precision. A novel approach to evaluating loop integrals called numerical causal depiction (NCD) is presented. Based on the topological structure of these integrals and the Feynman trick, the integrals are expressed as high-dimensional numbers dependent on the loop momentum and Cayley kernels. Standard integration techniques cannot directly apply due to the non-trivial causal domain. The non-trivial boundaries are addressed with hit-and-run algorithms in multiple dimensions, enabling the conversion of these dependencies into gamma functions. The method's accuracy is confirmed by comparing results to traditional methods like sector-decimation and sector-iteration on complex three-loop topologies such as double box and smuon box integrals. Notably, the method even handles very complex topology with massive particles, such as the box integral with six masses, with computed ratios of amplitudes showing significant variations.

We derive a general eigenstate expansion formula for one-dimensional two-level quantum walks using time evolution properties, which can be used to analyze eigenstates and spectral measures. Applying this formula, we successfully calculate the complete spectrum and spectral measure for one-dimensional quantum walks with Hopf-Fibonacci Hamiltonians and determine the complete spectrum and spectral measure for one-dimensional and two-level quantum walks with general periodic Hamiltonians as open-sided or both ends sealed systems accordingly.

This study examines the structure of stars containing quark matter with quark interactions modeled initially by the Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model and later supplemented by a color superconductivity gap and an omega-rho coupling.  A initial phase involves analyzing the pure quark star case under the influence of various Meissner effects, particularly at high densities.  These analyses reveal that introducing a superconductivity gap decreases the potential of the star's core, thus reducing its maximal mass.  Subsequently, we investigated the impact on hybrid stars consisting of an inner quark core surrounded by nuclear matter.  These hybrid stars were analyzed using the MIT bag model and found that variations in coupling constants significantly affect the predicted masses, particularly the mass of around 1.67 solar masses, suggesting potential evidence for the existence of these unusual stars, particularly those consisting of a quark core rather than a deconfined color rho mass core, based on observational findings.

In the presence of quantum noise originating from an ohmic environment, the occurrence of slow light phenomena is investigated using deformed optomechanical setups. The impact is assessed for two scenarios: one involving a driven probe field and another involving an undriven probe field. The study considers scenarios with driven damping and stochastic damping. The presence of deformed terms reduces the effectiveness of slowing down light but can be countered by increasing driving strength in the case of fast light observation. However, in the case of slow light generation via stochastic damping, reducing the influence of deformed terms is essential. Notably, reducing both the bath spectral density and the influence of deformed terms can yield a favorable figure of merit for both scenarios.

Adverse R-parity broken transitions, specifically R-parity broken scissors modes, have been explored within the Dual-rotors Model framework. Within its boundaries, adverse R-parity broken transitions, AdS states, emerge as a mixture of tensor rotator excitation and an odd deformation of the dual-rotors system. A comprehensive investigation of the dual-rotors Hamiltonian revealed that it can be adapted to accommodate tensor rotator and deformation excitation interactions. Using this modified Hamiltonian, we computed the energies of adverse R-parity broken and scissors modes, which were subsequently compared experimentally. Results demonstrate that the model accurately predicts scissors mode energy differences between stable and isomers and that isomers exhibit adverse R-parity broken states at higher energies than their stable counterparts.

Understanding the dynamics of rotation and orbital variations in ultrathin zoelite films requires modeling these variations using specific parameters, such as high rotation rates (large G) and varying orbital eccentricities (various e's). These parameters significantly impact the stability and complex behavior of film growth and structure. We've identified distinct patterns and intricate relationships between these parameters, revealing complex zoological behavior. Our analysis indicates that rotation rate has a substantial effect on film structure, with significant differences observed, especially when eccentricity is present. The aim of this work is to extract essential principles and rules from our detailed analysis to inform our knowledge of these unique oxide thin films.

We explore the impact of dissipation on the distribution patterns of
microscopically cooled atoms in optical arrays. By analyzing the joint position
distribution of $N$ atoms in a thermal state, we find that dissipation can lead
to the atom's position probabilities decreasing with the number of atoms, which
is contrary to the typical behavior where they increase. Our study shows that
this unique distribution pattern is most pronounced when the cooling rate and the
array's spatial periodicity are comparable. Additionally, we investigate the
atoms' behavior one at a time and discover that the distribution patterns in the
individual atoms' motion exhibit sub-Poissonian characteristics within the
thermal regime, which indicates the presence of correlations among the atoms.
Such correlations arise from interplay among cooling, spontaneous emission, and
array dynamics, all of which are heavily influenced by dissipation.

A study examining the cryptocurrency trading market analyzed both pairwise correlations and higher-order net skew correlations among cryptocurrencies. 
When examining the influence of news on correlations, researchers found significant impacts corresponding to major global events, such as the Brexit and the US presidential election. 
Interestingly, the study also revealed the existence of non-linear correlations, particularly stronger correlations among coins susceptible to similar market influences. 
These findings highlight the importance of exploring higher-order correlations within financial markets, as they can provide a more comprehensive understanding of their complex dynamics.

In the context of extremely small molecular clusters where the protons are highly dynamic, importance sampling zero-point energy corrections become crucial. These corrections are now being incorporated into theoretical models to better match the observations made by researchers using infrared spectroscopy and quantum mechanics. The development of these corrections involves methods such as path integrals, where the zero-point energy is considered through phase space configurations. The resulting importance sampling correction can be compared to traditional vibrational mode analysis, where significant modes are identified to calculate energy corrections. The accuracy of these corrections is being verified by comparing them to the full configuration interaction approach, allowing the assessment of when the inclusion of specific modes yields accurate results for the water-sulfuric acid cluster.

This study investigates the properties of recognition pairs $(X,Y)$ where $X$ is a compact space, focusing on recognizing when such pairs map into other compact recognition pairs $(X',Y')$. The results show that under certain conditions – specifically when $X'$ is F-dynastic and both $Y'$ and $Y$ are closed under certain transformations – the image of the morphism will have a specific structure relative to $X'$ and $Y'$. The concepts of recognition pairs are deeply rooted in the topology of group equivariant non-expansive functions between spaces, a field with significant applications in metric topology and geometric group theory. Recognisation pairs serve as an essential tool in metric topology, with its origins found in early work on isometric embeddings and expansions. These ideas are directly linked to other geometric group theory concepts, including quasi-isometric invariants, Lipschitz homology, and Lipschitz cohomology. Recognition pairs have also contributed to other invariants developed in these fields that are resistant to smooth changes.

In one spatial dimension, we establish that the thermal Hall response in insulating systems is a topologically determined property. Our analysis demonstrates that the periphery of these systems contributes a fixed thermal Hall conductance value, equivalent to eight times that contributed by the bulk. This discovery leads to the formulation of two crucial theorems for 1D thermal transport: (a) insulating systems that mimic Einstein relations possess a thermal Hall response; and (b) the thermal Hall response in such systems reaches its minimum possible value. This proof bypasses the long-standing theoretical hurdles by leveraging the thermal topological invariant, previously used to explain the quantized thermal topological insulator's peripheral thermal current generation. Our results reinforce the thermal Hall response as a reliable signature for characterizing thermal topological phases and highlight its potential for related technological applications.

When trained using various techniques, neural networks exhibit different behaviors influenced by geometric properties of data and model parameters, all acting as implicit regularizers that influence the final model outcome. This research focuses on understanding the underlying reasons for the simplicity of final models, considering multiple geometric factors that are influenced by data, labels, and network architecture, rather than viewing model complexity as the sole regularizer. Through controlled experiments and connections with theoretical models, the influence of different geometric factors is measured and analyzed, revealing that label quality has the most significant impact, followed by the arrangement of data, and then the model architecture. This new perspective allows us to develop models that are more robust and generalize better.

Assessing Wilson coefficients in $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays typically involves comparing theoretical predictions with experimental data, but this process often relies on uncertain form factors. A new method using measured rates and angular parameters enables us to directly estimate the interference term related to a specific Wilson coefficient combination without relying on theory. Applying this technique to the $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decay, we analyze data from the LHCb experiment's Run 2, covering q^2 ranges of 4.5-8, 6-8, and 5.5-8 GeV^2, and we observe no significant deviation from the Standard Model in these ranges.

Automated essay evaluation using automated writing evaluation systems (AWES) has become possible with significant advancements in natural language processing.  To improve the accuracy of EW systems, research has explored data enhancement methods.  This study evaluates the effectiveness of various data enhancement methods utilizing transformation-based architectures, including Transformer models, in enhancing the performance of EW systems, specifically the Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory with Attention model.  Experiments were performed on the 2017 National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) writing assessment, examining the effects of copying, translation, and synthetic data generation methods.  Notably, the study found that copying an essay's response to multiple times under different prompt variations using Transformer-based models significantly improved performance beyond previously established benchmarks, demonstrating the potential of these models in EW applications.

As extreme weather events escalate in frequency and intensity due to climate change, there's an urgent need to forecast severe conditions such as intense rainfall, heatwaves, and cold spells with heightened accuracy. This demand necessitates tracking the probability of exceeding temperature and rainfall thresholds, as well as understanding how temperature patterns on a grid influence each other, which can be achieved through the analysis of conditional extreme values and extremal dependence. This paper aims to introduce and categorize methods for examining and representing the relationship between extreme occurrences, as well as the development of tools for testing the validity of these methods in real-world scenarios.

This research examines how intergenerational mobility might change as access to opportunities becomes more widely available, using a dynamic model. The model incorporates several key aspects: families make long-term investments in opportunities across generations, opportunities can be shared and transferred, and access to opportunities has lasting effects on occupational attainment. The study reveals that broadening opportunity access can have two opposing effects on mobility: it can both increase and decrease mobility depending on the circumstances, and this dual nature is explained through a mid-point distinction: below a certain point, expanding opportunities tends to boost mobility, while above that point, it can have the opposite effect, and we show that these contrasting trends can be resolved.

The parity operator is employed to derive key connections between spin, statistics, and relativity. A crucial relationship, $(-1)^{2j} = \pm 1$, determines whether a particle is bosonic or fermionic based on its spin ($j$) and parity ($\pm 1$). This theoretical framework is showcased through an example using two bosons interacting through an s-wave potential. Our approach successfully covers both fermions and bosons, as well as particles with unusual parity configurations.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports delegated signing, allowing signers to be distributed across a group while avoiding exposure to DoS attacks through secret sharing. This results in negligible communication between signers, enabling transaction confirmation speeds comparable to transaction submission speeds. Additionally, we present performance improvements for multioutput transactions by optimizing input selection and output computation processes. Benchmarks show our delegation scheme outperforms current implementations, even those utilizing parallel computation, at multi-gigahertz server speeds.

This study investigates the difficulty of solving various types of linear equations within space complexity constraints, specifically focusing on simpler variants of NP-complete problems. By examining their toughness in terms of space complexity, this research incorporates problems such as 2-SAT and 2-CSP. Using a generalized form of Baker-Gill-Stewart's diagonalization technique, each of these problems is shown to have a distinct upper bound on its space complexity requirement, with 2-SAT potentially solvable in O(log n) space. Furthermore, this space complexity challenge is proven irreducible even with just two variables. This investigation deepens our understanding of space complexity and its relation to other computational models.

Using combined proton collision data from the CMS experiment at the LHC with 13 TeV energy and 102 inverse femtosecond seconds luminosity, we've examined the production of three massive gauge bosons in various final state combinations. Our analysis covers the simultaneous creation of two W bosons and one Z boson, two Z bosons and a W boson, and simultaneously all three gauge bosons as well, each with at least one being neutral. Our findings are in accordance with the Standard Model predictions for these processes. Additionally, we set strict upper limits on new physics scenarios beyond the Standard Model, specifically non-symmetrical and symmetric dark matter annihilations that result in multiple gauge bosons, setting some of the most rigorous constraints to date on the processes involving two W bosons and a Z boson annihilating and simultaneously all three gauge bosons annihilating.

Hebrew lacks widely accepted writing standards, resulting in significant orthographic variation, which poses challenges for NLP tasks. In this paper, we address this issue by presenting a second generation of Hebrew-based UD corpora. The first generation, comprising the Hebrew-treebank v2, Web语料库 v2, and Masoretic Text v2, emerged around 2018. We enhance the previous works by rectifying existing annotation issues, adopting latest NLP standards, and adopting Web语料库 v3's annosim annotation scheme. We then introduce new UD corpora, complementing the first generation with more accurate and methodically annotated data. Additionally, we develop cutting-edge models for Hebrew parsing, achieving remarkable results, outperforming existing models by a substantial 4.2 F1-points on the Hebrew-treebank development set. Our approach surpasses the best non-heuristic models in the UD pipeline, and we make the corpora and code publicly available for future reference.

We prove the existence of maps that significantly reduce dimension while almost perfectly preserving distances. Specifically, given a subset of the incompressible $l_p$ space with fractional dimension $\delta$, we show that in three specific ranges of $\p$, there are incompressible subsets of this set whose dimensions are reduced by a factor linearly related to $\delta$ under the influence of an incompressibility parameter $\ep$. These maps both shrink distances by at most a factor of two and expand them by at most a factor of $1+\ep$. Our research builds on earlier work by Naor and Scully as well as ideas presented at their conference.

Recent developments in machine learning have led to the emergence of data-informed modeling, which combines the strengths of physics-based and data-driven methods. This new approach addresses the limitations of purely data-driven methods, which struggle with generalizability and interpretation due to their lack of underlying physical principles. By integrating fundamental physical laws with machine learning, data-informed modeling enhances the generalizability and interpretability of these models. Furthermore, this methodology minimizes the amount of required training data and ensures that the models adhere to physical laws, thereby improving their reliability and credibility among domain experts. This paper explores the principles and advantages of data-informed modeling, which becomes particularly valuable in collaborative settings where model transparency and domain expertise play crucial roles.

We created novel rateless LDPC codes termed degree-degree related low-density parity-check (DDRLDPC) codes, featuring a unique property where the degree profiles of column and row are interconnected. Our simulations show that DDRLDPC codes significantly outperform conventional LDPC codes in terms of erasure recovery performance and complexity, particularly when they match the same average degree profile. Additionally, we developed an innovative erasure recovery algorithm tailored for DDRLDPC codes, adapting and building upon belief propagation (BP) and marginal probability propagation (MPP). Our proposals include two simplified recovery methods, additive BP (ABP) and truncated additive BP (TABP), which add a rank constraint to the BP system of linear equations. Our research reveals that DDRLDPC codes effectively resist the flooding phenomenon and exhibit superior performance compared to LDPC codes under high erasure rates. Our results demonstrate that the proposed erasure recovery algorithms for DDRLDPC codes, including ABP and TABP, outperform BP and MPP by being simpler and more efficient, as they require fewer iterations to achieve the same erasure recovery success rate.

This work addresses the challenge of safeguarding complex systems against malicious attacks that could lead to dangerous failures, such as excessive stress on major components or catastrophic system collapse. The proposed solution employs a predictive filter based on System Level Synthesis to monitor complex systems and anticipate stress levels in major components before they exceed safe thresholds. By analyzing historical data, the system learns to recognize patterns of attacks and adapts its security measures accordingly. The predictive filter incorporates model predictive control to restrict future behavior within a predefined safe region and verifies that stress levels on key components remain within acceptable bounds. To validate the effectiveness of the filter, a laboratory-based system was tested with sudden changes in load and deliberate failures. The system successfully prevented stress levels on important components from exceeding their safety limits.

We're presenting a new type of attack against the decoy-state quantum key distribution system, which works even with only partial phase randomization of the signal states. By accurately manipulating Bob's single-photon detection events and perfectly mimicking public communication, we can exploit the key generation process associated with four-detection events from Bob, ultimately achieving a 100% extraction of the generated key. This demonstrates that even with some level of phase randomization, part of the key remains vulnerable to attack. Our proposed attack will serve as a warning for system designers and implementation teams to fully guarantee phase randomization in decoy-state QKD system deployments.

Recent breakthroughs in large language models have significantly advanced the field of NLP. This new approach, known as in-context learning, allows for improved model performance and better exploration of its capabilities and limitations. Our study investigates the influence of various pretraining datasets on a model's ability to perform in-context learning, focusing on the scale, domain, and method of pretraining. Results from the experiment show that a model's domain of pretraining greatly affects its ICL ability in related tasks, while task-related pretraining can lead to a model's "overfitting" of those tasks, causing poor generalization. This overfitting phenomenon, however, can be mitigated through the use of a larger pretraining corpus and diverse data, emphasizing the need for a balanced approach to model training that prioritizes both domain-specific and general scales of data.

Our research focuses on understanding how galaxy clusters form and evolve by studying the effect of their central regions' fragmentation into smaller pockets of gas. To achieve this, we performed high-resolution simulations incorporating the influence of radiative cooling, field line topology, radiation hydrodynamics, and conduction mechanisms. We discovered that general relativistic effects have a significant impact on the formation of stable cores in galaxy clusters, particularly when radiative cooling outpaces the Hubble expansion. In our experiments, we analyzed the influence of magnetic field configurations and strength on the development of the central regions' gas pockets. We found that discrete cells of gas are formed due to the interplay of fluid instabilities and the growth of jets from supermassive black holes at the hearts of galaxies. Furthermore, our results revealed that fragmented gas morphology can trigger the growth of these black holes and potentially lead to the hot-wet-bright state observed in some galaxy clusters. To validate the accuracy of our simulation methods, we validated them by comparing the results with existing X-ray observations of galaxy clusters, including RXCJ0311.8-0254, and identified the conditions necessary to replicate the observed fragmented gas patterns.
The measurement of CP discrepancies in beauty and charm particles has been addressed.

Expanding upon the recently proposed Ramanujan's Gross conjecture for superstring theory, we explore its application to the long-standing problem of deriving a general formula for the $n$-point bosonic scattering amplitude in the context of the four-dimensional gauge theory arising from the string. Our work extends the conjecture to include the $n$-point scattering amplitudes, $A_n$, in direct alignment with the Gross-Siegel recursive relations. We present the Gross conjecture in an innovative expression, presenting it as $A_n=\frac{\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n-3}}0^n_{0}z_{0}z_{\infty}z_{\sigma(3)}z_{\sigma(4)}\cdots z_{\sigma(n-1)}}{\sum_{\sigma\tilde{\sigma}\in S_{n-3}\times S_{n-3}}z_{\sigma(3)}\tilde{z}_{\tilde{\sigma}(3)}\cdots z_{\sigma(n-1)}\tilde{z}_{\tilde{\sigma}(n-1)}}$.

As 5G networks approach deployment, their deployment, operations, and maintenance present new challenges. To overcome these, the concept of Self-Org. Cell. Net. is being explored, where the networks themselves manage and monitor their own organized operations. To achieve this, a central management system provides essential processes that enable the networks to be self-managing, with particular focus on services related to 5G's Deployment, Planning, and Resource Allocation. Using a prototype of this central management system, we demonstrate how the incorporated mechanisms enable an efficient, cost-effective, sustainable, and reliable management of 5G Cell. self-managed networks.

Current state-of-the-art voice synthesis systems rely on extensive datasets of unlabeled audio recordings paired with transcripts to function effectively. These systems fail for individuals who have no existing data available, as gathering suitable data for these individuals is often an impractically time-consuming and costly endeavor. To overcome this limitation, we have created a novel approach that leverages extremely limited data points to create voice models by mapping a resource-free audio individual to a data-rich individual through transcripts based on perceptual auditory units. Our method enables the accurate replication of the target voice characteristics even with just two available samples. The reliability of our synthesis system can additionally be enhanced by incorporating additional constraints that reflect the constraints imposed by human auditory perception.

We approach the motion planning problem in differentiated habitats as a multi-stage optimization issue involving multiple convex sub-problems that need appropriate linking mechanisms. By utilizing input data informed by an analytical breakdown, we apply the McCormick envelope technique to develop tight relaxations that effectively constrain the problems' feasible movements. Our method leverages pre-computed analytical solutions and runtime adjustments to produce reliable and precise approximations of the problems' convex representations. Furthermore, we integrate data-driven techniques to further refine and benchmark our solutions under varying conditions. This setup enables multiple capabilities, including reliable hot-starting of the problems and progressive refinement over successive iterations. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in delivering precise approximations and achieving rapid convergence within significant timeframes, all while maintaining transparency into the optimization process.

We examine the concept of converting one quantum state to another under specific constraints. In an ideal scenario, two quantum channels are regarded as equivalent when one can be used to transform any input state to its desired output statistically independently. However, this relationship does not conform to a strictly ordered system, allowing us to establish distinct state classifications according to their transformability possibilities. Our research demonstrates that, under strict criteria, only fundamental invariant properties of quantum states facilitate the deterministic transformation of states. These newly discovered properties have implications in various fields, such as communication complexity, statistical hypothesis testing, and estimation, where they yield improved bounds than previously achieved through traditional stochastic transformation rules.

We've successfully recreated the movement of a liquid in a cup by using a dropper on a mechanically swinging arm in a full-filled coffee cup. By using a computer-controlled system, we moved the coffee in a plane and captured images of the flow by taking high-speed photos. Our images showed complex fluid patterns including vortexes that formed due to the movement of the coffee's surface. Our study provides a simpler way to study the flow of viscous liquids by using a mechanical pendulum instead of the traditional mechanized splash.

Distributed machine learning has gained significant traction in scenarios involving massive datasets that are stored across multiple devices, thanks to advancements in hardware and software. The stochastic gradient descent method has become a widely-used teaching algorithm in such scenarios. However, its effectiveness can be compromised by discrepancies in data distributions among devices, necessitating the development of more resilient alternatives. Furthermore, when communication between devices is characterized by slow links and complex topologies, achieving consensus through consensus-based approaches like DR-Distributed SGD (DSGD) may become impractical due to slow convergence. To address these challenges, a new device-aware decentralized teaching algorithm, DR-DSGD, is proposed, which incorporates device awareness into the Distributed SGD framework to mitigate distribution discrepancies and slow communication effects, resulting in improved generalization performance. DR-DRGD draws inspiration from DR-Distributed SGD, introducing device bias corrections and deviation-based loss functions. By theoretical analysis and empirical validation, DR-DRGD demonstrates superior generalization performance compared to existing decentralized and distribution-robust teaching algorithms, outperforming them significantly in both non-IID settings and scenarios involving slow communication.

We demonstrate that utilizing flow components and initial state particle distributions allows for the estimation of crucial collision parameters without relying on longitudinal directions or final state data. A simple relationship indicates that using elliptical flow components and coefficients enables the determination of collision deformation. Moreover, certain properties remain unchanged from initial to final states. By applying this approach to data from gold-gold collisions at various energies, we found evidence that only high-energy collisions significantly affected the collision duration. Furthermore, applying our method to proton-saturn collisions revealed that these collisions generally produced smaller and shorter-lived collisions, with some exceptions. Additionally, this approach helps determine the average transverse mass of produced particles.

Observations from ALMA reveal that while low-speed outflows are commonly observed in young stars, high-speed protostellar jets are becoming increasingly rare. A prevailing theory suggests that these slow-moving jets should be abundant, yet they haven't been widely recorded, leading researchers to question their true nature. Some have even proposed that these jets could contribute to the dissemination of carbon-chain molecules in molecular clouds, but this idea remains controversial. We examined this hypothesis through detailed numerical simulations, modeling the interaction between hot wind and cooler, diffuse gas, focusing on chemical reactions and particle collisions. Our results show that the energy from these low-speed outflows is insufficient to significantly influence the distribution of high-speed jets, carbon-rich gas, or to generate the observed maser emissions, suggesting that these complex particle collisions do not explain the observed phenomena.

This paper examines a fundamental challenge in engineering systems known as constrained nonlinear control. Traditionally, control strategies prioritize stability and efficiency. Yet in today's constrained environments, additional priorities such as resource conservation and environmental impact must be considered. Equilibrated regulation control offers a comprehensive approach that addresses these diverse demands, ensuring systems operate within specified limits while maintaining optimal performance beyond those boundaries. This paper presents an equilibrated regulation law, proven equivalence with other well-established control methods, and successful application in controlling a constrained nonlinear system, demonstrating its potential for broader constrained nonlinear control applications.

Orbital resonances in the gravitational interaction between the Sun and bodies modeled by elliptical orbits occur periodically. Certain semi-secular resonances are critical because they significantly impact the orbital dynamics, particularly those affecting solar system particles such as zodiacal light. This study employs various analytical and numerical techniques to develop efficient and precise approximations of resonance functions and assesses their performance using statistical analysis,yielding fast and accurate evaluations of these functions even on basic computing devices. The proposed methods include an optimal polynomial approximation approach, transfer function technique, and alternative algorithms. The results show that these approximations perform comparably to existing methods, such as those by Chazaran et al.优异的精度和速度. The developed analytical and numerical solutions are applied to model the orbital behavior of a resonant particle, taking into account factors like orbital eccentricity, oblatness coefficients, and mean anomaly, revealing that such resonances lead to the exchange of eccentricity and inclination, characterized by the倾角 index increasing monotonically. The study demonstrates that new and existing approximations effectively capture the temporal evolution of resonance functions, particularly their amplitude decay and the shift in zero crossing time.

We examine the symmetry of light-matter interactions within typical model Hamiltonians used in tight-binding simulations. Our analysis reveals that both the electric dipole and Stark models exhibit invariance under spatial translations, rotations, and dilations combined with a frequency shift. This inherent symmetry implies the presence of a conserved continuity equation, representing the system's total energy. By establishing a continuity equation duality framework, we demonstrate that only tight-binding models which are measure invariance possess a positive-definite energy spectrum, making them suitable for studying the optical properties of condensed matters. Our framework also enables the efficient computation of frequency-dependent dielectric functions through time-dependent density functional theory, along with a generalization of existing theorem-based approaches to handle broad frequency ranges from first-principle tight-binding models.

Our focus is on achieving category-level object perception in dynamic environments, with the goal of identifying objects that behave similarly across different contexts and categories. We define perception as the ability to identify objects regardless of their class and understand their shape and position. We identify key points in 3D space that represent a specific object class, which serve as a basis for perception. We then present a novel system that perceives objects in both 2D images and 3D scenes, which can detect objects in 3D scenes and predict their position accurately. Moreover, we define and tackle the challenge of perceiving objects in Adversarial 3D Scenes, which are designed to distort 3D sensor data and deceive object detection. We demonstrate that our system successfully detects and shapes objects in these adverse conditions using over 1000 object classes from 3D datasets.

This study introduces a novel interval estimation technique based on mutual recursion principles for parameters of a Cauchy distribution. We derive precise formulas for constructing confidence regions, which can be further simplified into confidence intervals under certain conditions, such as symmetry. The method's performance is evaluated through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, comparing its statistical properties with those of the maximum likelihood estimation approach.

A statistical method utilizing Bayesian data-lending techniques in multi-arm clinical trials can reduce sample size while maintaining trial power.  One prominent example is the graphical borrowing approach used in trials comparing multiple new treatments to a control.  We enhance this method to accommodate trials structured in groups, known as basket trials, which conduct similar evaluations across various gene or disease categories.  Our improved technique enables shared data between subsets within these basket trials.  Using two fictional basket trial examples, we compare our graphical method with alternative approaches.  Our results show that our graphical method has the potential to reduce sample sizes compared to standard non-borrowing trials and significantly increase power compared to methods that exclude partially incompatible data.

To create highly accurate motion systems, we use control systems that can be adjusted based on their characteristics. By organizing these controls in a sequential manner and independently tuning each component, we simplify the process. However, due to the dependence of a system's behavior on its operating conditions, simply arranging the controls isn't sufficient to create stable controls for all scenarios. Our proposed method incorporates a scheduling system to switch controls based on the operating conditions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method with a table that allows for adjustments in acceleration and acceleration rates. Results show that this method yields better accuracy and is easier to set up compared to uncontrollable alternatives.

Deep learning registration methods benefit significantly from complete spatial data, which real-world partial observations often lack. Consequently, these observations pose significant registration challenges. Existing approaches employ various heuristic sampling methods that require extensive hyperparameter tuning and perform poorly when facing complex scenarios and deformable objects. These issues motivate the development of registration methods capable of adaptively selecting relevant points based on the observed geometric features. We introduce self-guided learning for partial-to-partial registration, where regression networks predict soft weights for points and triangles to reflect their importance and guide the matching process. We develop corresponding sampling and matching modules to adhere to the predicted soft weights, and further refine them through continuous relaxation operations to simplify the optimization process. Experimental validation on synthetic and medical datasets demonstrates the advantages of our method.

Building upon previous work by Kim, Li, and Zhao, we broaden their findings concerning the $R_\infty$-characteristic of Baumslag-Solitar groups to encompass nilpotent quotients of these groups, and distinct proofs are provided, including a more direct method for determining the invariant in such quotients, and an alternative proof leveraging the group's Gromov boundary infinity characteristic. Moreover, our work establishes a link with bi-orderable groups and their left-invariant total orders having the $R_\infty$-characteristic.

The possibility of challenging the long-term stability of the electroweak vacuum within the Standard Model is largely dependent on high-energy particle physics collar collisions. To achieve this, researchers have developed a theoretical framework that allows for the quantification of a country's potential to produce unstable vacuum transitions. This "framework at the collider" can be utilized to determine the most suitable facility for first-hand investigation into vacuum instability, regardless of the specific transition energy outcome. According to this framework, the optimal design parameters for a collider intended to probe a phenomenon are those that maximize the product of its transition production cross-section and the associated lepton pair decay probability. This is achieved through high-luminosity collisions at an energy approximately 1.2 times the transition energy, with narrowest possible width. As such, the ideal collider would likely be a high-luminosity, energy-tunable linear $e^-e^+$ collider, with a capacity of at least 10 ab$^{-1}$ per year. This framework can be applied to any set of SM parameters, and by incorporating two-Higgs-doublet models and supersymmetric models, it suggests that a $e^-e^+$ collider with a 250 GeV center of mass energy and 10$^{34}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ luminosity is necessary to conduct a thorough investigation into the vacuum's long-term stability, with a data collection period of at least a year.

A novel trajectory framework has been developed to reverse the effects of temporal resolution in ultra-fast spectroscopy. The newly devised algorithm segmentizes the reverse-time evolution of a physical system and adjusts these segments to replicate the recorded intensity patterns. By employing an efficient optimization technique, the framework establishes that system reversal is feasible only when there is sufficient time-resolution, and presents a robust method that converges from various starting points. The framework is showcased through its application to the analysis of ethylene photochemistry and sapphire signal attenuation, and successfully recovers accurate dynamics and interaction strengths that align with established quantum chemical calculations. Furthermore, the framework's application to specific materials demonstrates its capability to handle complex systems involving non-adiabatic transitions, anharmonicity, and electronic excitations. The framework's success highlights the potential of leveraging this method to gain deeper understanding of time-resolved spectroscopic data, particularly in cases where traditional reconstruction methods may struggle.

The challenge in analyzing extremely narrow decay potentialities of excited charm mesons suggests a necessity to examine their Bethe-Salpeter component structures. Therefore, we compute these components for the excited $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ vector mesons using the asymptotic worldline spectrum method. This computation enables us to derive unique Fock-space scale-dependent wave functions, ultimately enabling the calculation of complex lepton decay coefficients. The study also involves a comparative analysis with existing lattice results. The findings reveal that the twist-3 vector lepton decay coefficients exhibit notable discrepancies relative to conventional perturbative QCD predictions. Additionally, the research shows that these differences may be partially mitigated by incorporating certain particle-antiparticle loop contributions.

We derive descriptive  Fourier characters for the Shilov boundary of sectors and polydiscs across various dimensions. Our work shows that the Shilov boundary can be identified as the only subset with non-trivial Fourier characters within specific space expansions used to define Gelfand-Shilov spaces. Furthermore, we utilize these characterizations to investigate Toeplitz operators applied to these shilov spaces.

Instance division serves as a fundamental unsupervised learning technique that enables knowledge representation and data visualization without the need for labeled data from multiple modalities. By generating cross-modal alignments and evaluating them through unsupervised metrics, this method produces partitions of datasets into semantically distinct groups. Nevertheless, these partitions frequently lack accuracy due to suboptimal clustering of cross-modal data. To address this limitation, we present an improved framework that integrates generator-based partitioning with discriminator-driven adversarial refinement in a cyclic setup. The framework employs multiple discriminators to assess cross-modal correspondences and leverages cyclic adversarial training to optimize these correlations. Notably, this approach necessitates labeling only a subset of cross-modal pairs to assign them to distinct branches for supervised learning within each branch. The proposed framework is demonstrated by splitting datasets of unlabelled clothing images and successfully producing accurate clothing categories after incorporating a single batch of garment images.

This paper investigates how to optimize the balance between increased features and higher computational costs in Recurrent Neural Networks. We utilize Kernelization and understand its impact on the vanishing gradient problem, analyzing its effects on training dynamics. It's demonstrated that using kernelized functions for engineered features leads to better generalization of deep RNNs, particularly in action prediction tasks, with minimal additional computational cost. As a result, we present a new model called RBF-KFM-RNN that combines these concepts with a RNN with Radial Basis Functions for feature mapping.

During its unprecedented 1985 outburst, AD Leo exhibited significant changes in its ultraviolet spectrum that we have analyzed. By comparing observed data from Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Telescope and Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 on Hubble Space Telescope, we found substantial discrepancies, indicating substantial near-ultraviolet emission. Furthermore, analysis of 1985 ultraviolet lines revealed a complex interplay between accretion processes and wind phenomena, suggesting a less active wind compared to typical outbursts, yet still accompanied by a blue continuum likely originating from the accretion shock itself.

We explore deformations of G2-instantons on nearly G2 manifolds with symmetry, focusing on the role of the Killing vector field. The study reveals that the space of variations of the connection of such an instanton can be decomposed into two distinct subspaces. The first consists of trivial variations, which stem from the Lie derivative of the connection form along the Killing vector field. The second comprises non-trivial variations, which correspond to sections of the twisted first Hilbert-Schmidt ideal Dirac operator. A specific criterion is established to determine when an instanton is rigid. Additionally, this investigation reveals connections to the existence problem for G2-instantons, particularly in the case of S2 x H2 torus actions on nearly G2 structures, where such instances are shown to fail.

This study investigates the distribution of the orbits of nearly all analytic functions on the unit disk under the action of C-normal weighted composition operators with analytic symbols and additive surjective semigroup mappings, demonstrating their evenness and continuity. As a result, we establish that the orbits are dense in H^2 and the space l^2 H^2. Furthermore, we demonstrate the occurrence of uniform distribution within H^2 and l^2 H^2 under specific conditions of the weights.

The concept of big p-core numbers was introduced based on the analysis of partition frequencies with p-core characteristics. These numbers correspond exactly to the count of specific walks starting from zero on the additive residue graph of order p. Building upon existing research regarding big 2-core 3-configurations, this paper examines these walks for arbitrary powers of p. Utilizing a specialized substitution method, we derive generating functions for big p-core numbers and analyze their asymptotic behavior.

We propose a novel approach, Transformation-Unique Smoothing, that leverages the inherent characteristics of Local Geometric Structure in point clouds to achieve high-quality 3D object reconstruction from a limited number of views. Our method tackles the critical challenge of eliminating noise and artifacts on the Local Geometric Structure of intermediate multi-view surface models without compromising the fine details. By maintaining local geometric features, our intrinsic smoothing method generates high-fidelity surface models that can be effectively used for cross-view smoothening. Furthermore, we introduce the ABSS-IOU metric, a evaluation standard for assessing cross-view smodel quality, and surpass existing approaches by an average of 10% in terms of performance. Our superior results are publicly available for research purposes.

We investigate media access methods in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks within distributed distributed sensing applications. This research develops and evaluates novel radar network protocols adapted from common network access methods, specifically slotted ALOHA and CSMA. A key constraint of FMCW radars is that they cannot be rapidly switched on and off, which significantly restricts the implementation of media access methods. Consequently, we introduce a specialized protocol of slotted ALOHA with an extended time frame. This scheme divides time into discrete slots, with each slot comprising a distinct network operation: either a target detection phase or a ranging phase.
